PREFACE
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Health and
Family Welfare, having been authorized by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf, hereby
present this Sixty- second Report of the Committee on Action T aken by Government on the
Recommendations/Observations contained in the Committee’s 57
th Report on Demands for Grants
2012-13 (Demand No. 49) of the Department of AIDS Control, Ministry of Health and Family
Welfare for the year 2012-13.
2. The Fifty-s eventh Report of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on
Health and Family Welfare was presented to Rajya and laid on the Table of Lok Sabha on 26 th and
25th April, 2012 respectively. Replies of the Government on the recommendations contained in the
Report, received from the Department of AIDS Control were considered by the Committee at its
meeting held on the 8 th February, 2013 .
3. The Committee considered the Draft Report and adopted the same in its meeting held on the
8th February, 2013.
 BRAJESH PATHAK

recommendations contained in its Fifty-seventh Report on Demands for Grants (Demand No. 49)
of the Department of AIDS Control for the year 2012-13.
2. Action Taken Notes have been received from the Government in respect of the
recommendations contained in the Report. They have been categorized as follows:
(i) Recommendations/Observations in respect of which replies of the Government have
been accepted by the Committee: 1.8, 4.3, 5.4, 6.4, 6.5, 8.3, 8.4, 8.5, 8.7, 10.3,
11.3, 11.6, 11.8, 12.2, 13.3, Total–15 (Chapter I)
(ii) Recommendations/Observations in respect of which the Committee does not desire to
pursue in view of the Government’s replies: 1.1, 1.5, 1.6, 1.7, 2.6, 2.12, 2.13, 2.14,
3.2, 7.3(a), 7.3(b), 8.6, Total–12 (Chapter II)
(iii) Recommendations/Observations in respect of which replies of the Government have
not been accepted by the Committee: 2.10, 5.3, 5.7, 7.2, 9.2, 9.4, 14.4 Total–7
(Chapter III)
(iv) Recommendations/Observations in respect of which final replies of the Government
are still awaited: Nil, Total–Nil (Chapter-IV)
3. The details of the ATNs are discussed in various Chapters in the succeeding pages.

CHAPTER-I
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH REPLIES
OF THE GOVERNMENT HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE COMMITTEE
I. INTRODUCTION
CARE, SUPPORT AND TREATMENT
Recommendation/Observation
1.1 In Bihar, where HIV and visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar) interact and co-infection is a
problem, the Committee recommends as a first step-in areas that are endemic for Kala-azar –
Department of AIDS control should consider actively screening people living with HIV for this life-
threatening disease. Co-infected patients should then be given antiretrovirals as soon as possible
after starting anti-kala-azar therapy. (Para 1.8)
Action Taken
Visceral Leishmaniasis (kala – azar) is one of the disease which is endemic in the State of
Bihar. Kala-azar among HIV positive patients requires regular screening as it is regarded as one of
the Opportunistic Infections(OI) in endemic areas. Thus, at the time of pre-ART registration and
thereafter, all PLHIV are screened for such OIs and then referred to the diagnostic facilities
available under National Vector Borne Disease Control Programme for confirmatory diagnosis of
kala-azar. All PLHIV with co-infection of kala-azar are regarded as “WHO Clinical Stage – IV” as
per the existing case definition and are provided ART as soon as possible after starting anti kala-
azar therapy irrespective of CD4 count.
IV SETTING UP OF NEW BLOOD COMPONENT SEPARATION UNITS
Recommendation/Observation
1.2 The Committee appreciates that the targets set by the Department under NACP-III for
setting up of BCSUs have been achieved more or less. The Committee would, however, like to be
updated regularly of the targets set and success achieved by these units. (Para 4.2)
Action Taken
In the beginning of NACP III there was a target of setting up new BCSUs in 80 tertiary
care hospitals in addition to continuing support for 82 BCSUs which already existed.
As of date (June 2012), all of the proposed 80 centers are licensed.
The targets have been achieved with efforts of close follow up by the programme for
obtaining site allocation by the state, equipment installation, allocation of funds as per pattern of
assistance, follow up with the office of DCG(I) for central license at all stages.

Recommendation/Observation
1.3 The Committee notes that not only quantity but also quality matters. Blood transfusion is
life-saving treatment in many situations. But transfusions can also be a quick and easy route for
the transmission of infectious agents such as HIV , HBV , HCV , and malaria. NACO has been
entrusted the task of setting up and expanding blood banks across the country. Several studies
reviewing the current scenario in transfusion medicine (TM) in India indicate an urgent need for
restructuring the blood transfusion services with extreme variations in management and quality.
These studies note that compliance with quality assurance and GMP is not ensured. A large number
of blood banks are unlicensed. The Committee feels that since quality of blood banks is regulated
under the Drugs and Cosmetic Rules, under schedule ‘F’, Department of AIDS Control and the
DCGI should jointly come up with a plan to urgently address the issue of quality of blood banks
in the private and public sector. (Para 4.3)
Action Taken
NACO is focusing on quality management systems in Blood Banks in the country. Quality
management modules were prepared at NACO with the assistance of a group of experts in
Transfusion Medicine and Quality. These quality management modules are to be used in Blood
banks at the state level. So far 12 workshops covering 28 states for Quality Management have been
completed by NACO.
Efforts are also being made to monitor the blood banks and core committees have been
constituted in all states comprising Blood Bank experts and representative of the Drug Controller
at the state level, to monitor all blood banks.
Department of AIDS Control and the DCGI will also make a joint plan to execute the above
in a smooth manner.
Blood Transfusion service in the respective state is implemented by State level
functionaries. DCG (I) at the centre and its counterparts in the state are responsible for the
regulation and licensing of Blood Banks. Department of AIDS Control (DAC) is making all efforts
by working with the states and providing funds for augmenting voluntary blood donation and
ensuring provision of safe and quality blood in the country by reducing HIV transmission through
blood to < 0.5%.
V. SETTING UP OF NEW DISTRICT LEVEL BLOOD BANKS
Recommendation/Observation
1.4 The Committee also recommends to the Department to take special cognizance of the
underserved districts of Uttarakhand, Uttar Pradesh and Jharkhand. The Committee further
recommends that the Department should keep assessing the requirements of Blood Banks based on
the actual needs in various States due to migration and other factors. (Para 5.4)

4
Action Taken
NACO is taking special cognizance of the underserved areas including districts of
Uttarakhand, Uttar Pradesh and Jharkhand. NACO regularly assesses these states as per their
requirement for blood as per the population.
In Uttarakhand, support for a district level blood bank by NACO has been approved during
2012-13for the newly created district of Ranikhet. 21 newly created Blood Component separation
units of Uttar Pradesh are being given financial support of annual recurring grant in the financial
year 2012-13. In Jharkhand, NACO is taking initiatives for licensing of the three blood banks at
Saraikela, Chatra and Koderma.
VI. INTEGRATED COUNSELING AND TESTING CENTERS (ICTCS)
Recommendation/Observation
1.5 The Committee is at a loss to understand the rationale on the basis of which the
Department, in the first place fixes the target and fails to achieve the same year after year. A plain
reading of the target set vis-à-vis the achievement shows that the Department is not following its
own yardstick of fixing of target each year on the basis of achievement of the previous year,
which shows poor foresight of planning by the Department. The Committee, therefore, enjoins
upon the Department to seriously set realistic and achievable targets. Once targets are fixed, all
efforts should be made to achieve them. (Para 6.4)
Action Taken
As per the targets set under NACP III, the Department, through year wise scale up, had
to reach an end-line annual target of 22 million per year by the end of NACP III i.e. 2011-12. This
is inclusive of the target of counselling and testing of 75 lakh pregnant women.
To achieve this, the Department scaled up HIV counselling and testing facilities from 4567
in 2007-08 to 10,515 in 2011-12. Programme coverage has increased from 7.8 million in 2007-08
to 19.4 million in the year 2011-12.
During the year 2011-12 (April 2011 to March 2012) the Department has achieved the target
of counselling and testing 19.4 million attendees including 85.6 lakh pregnant women. Thus overall
achievement is 88% and the achievement of coverage of pregnant women is 113% as against the
target set for the last year of NACP III.
Recommendation/Observation
1.6 Testing of pregnant women raises several ethical questions. The Committee feels these
ethical issues have to be addressed at the time of rolling out routine testing of pregnant women
under NRHM. Testing with counseling is key. Support services for domestic violence and
discrimination within the family and community are also crucial. Treatment needs of women who
test positive should also be the top priority. Absence of these components will have an adverse
impact on the uptake of ante-natal services if they are identified with routine HIV testing of
pregnant women. The Committee feels that a detailed study on the testing of women who, are
pregnant – their treatment and the discrimination they face, – must be immediately undertaken and
should be used to shape a more sensitive and humane testing programme for pregnant women.
(Para 6.5)
Action Taken
Under the routine counseling and testing services for pregnant women provided under

5
NACP, all pregnant women are offered counseling and testing for HIV . These Pregnant women have
the right to “opt-out” under the existing strategy . Counseling is provided to all pregnant women
before and after HIV test. Any HIV positive pregnant women detected by the ICTCs is offered
PPTCT services and linked to Care Support and Treatment services.
The recommendations of the Committee for conducting a detailed study on testing of
women who are pregnant – their treatment and discrimination they face, will be taken up by the
Department.
VIII. ANTIRETROVIRAL TREATMENT (ART) CENTERS
Recommendation/Observation
1.7 The Committee notes that stockouts of ART medicines were reported throughout 2011 in
many states including UP, Bihar, Maharashtra, Manipur etc. The Committee fails to understand as
to how performance of RITES has been called satisfactory in such circumstances. The Committee
recommends that the Department take a more serious note of such lapses and have closer
monitoring mechanism in place since such gaps in supply only add to drug resistance apart from
the obvious inconvenience. (Para 8.3)
1.8 The Committee has noted that throughout 2011, there have been regular incidents of HIV
drug (first, Second and pediatric doses) in different States, which has been reported by different
PLHIV networks. The Committee feels that this is a serious issue since stock outs mean drug
interruptions which can lead to increased public health risks of HIV drug resistance. The
Committee recommends that an investigation and report be undertaken to list the numbers of
stock outs and to document the reasons for the stock outs. NACO should also outline to this
Committee what measures have been planned to prevent and to deal with incidents of stock outs.
The role of the PLHIV Networks should be to continue this good work of monitoring HIV
treatment at ART Centres and reporting problems like stock outs of NACO. PLHIV networks
should be further encouraged to continue reporting such incidents. Stock outs are related to
inefficiencies such as poor planning, incorrect projections of local requirements, poor distribution
and supply at treatment facilities, expiry of medicines as the stock that was received earlier is
not distributed first. The Committee recommends that NACO immediately reform the
pharmaceutical supply management system for HIV medicines as it is an important element in
treatment programmes. (Para 8.4)
Action Taken
As per the information captured in the Computerised Management Information System
(CMIS) under the programme, during 2011, 32 sites had shown stock-out of ARV drugs, most of
them only for few days. On detailed analysis, it was found that the stock out of ARV drugs for
more than a week was found only in 4 ART centres in two States of Uttar Pradesh and Bihar. The
corrective measures were initiated immediately by relocation from other ART centres with surplus
stocks.
Subsequently, in order to prevent such situation of stock-out of ARV drugs in future, NACO
has decentralised the allocation of ARV drugs through SACS instead of directly sending to ART
centres, so that State level monitoring of stocks is ensured.
Now each State AIDS Control Society has a designated official at the level of Joint Director
to ensure distribution and supply chain management of various ARV drugs in their respective States.
Further, NACO now has a dedicated Logistic Coordinator at the central level, which looks after
stock position and supply management of various ARV drugs in each State/UT.

6
A drug estimation committee has been constituted consisting of eminent medical specialists,
having expertise in the field for proper forecasting of ARV drugs, to ensure adequate quantity of
ARV drugs are indented for procurement.
In the State Grievance Redressal Committee meetings, which is constituted in every state,
the PLHIV network also participates as a member of the Committee. This Committee meets from
time to time and the feedback provided by the PLHIV networks is immediately acted upon by
initiating corrective measures including the issue of stock-out of ARV drugs at the ART centres.
Recommendation/Observation
1.9 The Committee feels that the slow rate of scale up of ART treatment over the last decade
has forced patients into the private sector where inappropriate HIV drug regimens are often
prescribed, leading to a long term public health problem of drug resistance. Many economic and
bureaucratic barriers have been noted in the eligibility criteria for enrolling in the programme for
those needing alternative first line or second line HIV drugs. As a result, patient groups have had
to approach the Supreme Court. These barriers must be addressed and must not be created for
patients who will need third line HIV medicines. Currently the proportion of HIV patients who have
failed to the second-line treatment is probably very small. The programme must start planning for
ART Centres of Excellence to take in these few patients. This will control drug resistance. Cost
alone should not be the only criteria. Failure to procure the third line drugs will have future public
health complications as PLHIVs could develop a very resistance HIV which could prove costly.
Planning and treating third line in a few patients will build capacity and experience of public health
facilities classified as centres of excellence by Department of AIDS Control. (Para 8.5)
Action Taken
It is submitted that ART was started in 2004 with 8 ART centres, which have been rapidly
scaled up to existing 355 centres (March 2012) against a target of setting up of 250 such ART
centres by 2012.
As per the information available with Deptt. of AIDS Control, only 35,000 patients are on
ART in private sector against around 5,42,000 patients in the public sector in the country.
As per the need of the programme, the second line ART was rolled out in two Centres of
Excellence (COE) in 2008 and was extended to 10 COEs and 18 ART Plus centres to expand this
service across the country. In addition, 7 COEs for Paediatric HIV Care are also providing the
services of second line ART.
The criteria for enrolling patients on second line were stringent as options for drugs in
management of HIV/AIDS were limited. This has helped in continuance of first line therapy to a
large number of patients who were failing due to factors other than drug resistance and actually
did not require the second line regimen. This has also provided a broader base of ARV drugs for
such patients who might require the same in future. The same approach was explained to Hon’ble
Supreme Court and as per directions, the criteria for inclusion of patients on treatment failure was
relaxed. Even after relaxation, the number of patients on second line ART is 4208 (as on March
2012) in all the designated centres.
All the COEs and ART Plus centres are well equipped to manage all types of patients on
HIV/AIDS care. As the HIV virus is constantly mutated, the Drug Resistance is not only related
to Treatment Adherence alone. As and when required and recommended by the Technical Resource
Group on ART, the programme will look into use of newer drugs for subsequent therapy (third line
ARV regimen) in public interest and with public health approach.

7
National AIDS Control Programme lays great emphasis on issues related to proper
counselling of patients to ensure complete adherence to treatment, so that patient do not develop
resistance early and continue the first line regimen as long as possible. The second line treatment
is also provided under NACP. The overall Drug Resistance in the country is very low and as of
now, there is no major public health threat of large number of PLHIV developing resistance to the
virus.
Recommendation/Observation
1.10 The Committee is constrained to observe that the Department has not treated the matter of
phasing out Stavudine with the urgency and seriousness it deserves. The Committee feels that the
inordinate delay on the part of the Department in this regard is a sad commentary on the working
of the Department and calls for introspection. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the
Department should start phasing out of Stavudine in a time bound manner. The Committee desires
to be kept apprised of the action taken in this regard. (Para 8.7)
Action Taken
The World Health Organisation (WHO) has released the guidelines for Antiretroviral Therapy
(ART) for HIV infection in adults and adolescents (2010 revision). The guidelines mainly describe
the newer strategies with regard to the starting of treatment and the drugs needed to be used at
the time to starting.The WHO also recommended country adaptation of these guidelines based on
the context of each country’s HIV epidemic, the strengths and weakness of health systems, and
the availability of financial, human and other essential resources.
WHO recommends phasing out of ARV drug Stavudine from ART regimen. Two meetings
of the Technical Resource Group on ART were held in Aug’ 10 and Dec’11to discuss this issue.
Subsequently, it was decided that Stavudine would be phased out from the national ART programme
for both existing and new patients. This phase out will be done once the drugs from the
procurement cycle of 2012-13 are in place. Thus, during 2012, phase out will start by not using
any Stavudine based regimen for new patients and later on the old patients will be shifted to non-
Stavudine based regimen in a phased manner.
X. ADOLESCENCE EDUCATION PROGRAMME (AEP)
Recommendation/Observation
1.11 The committee is impressed that with consistent efforts of the Department, the programme
is running in most of the States. The Committee feels that the Department should vigorously take
up with the States where the programme is still under suspension, the reasons for the delay in
implementation of the programme and resolve their apprehensions in this regard without any further
delay, in view of the fact that HIV/AIDS is a hydra headed monster which usually attacks the
vulnerable adolescent population due to lack of awareness of the devastating effects the diseases
could have on them. The states, that have suspended, should also reconsider their decision.
(Para 10.3)
Action Taken
Adolescence Education Programme (AEP) is promoted by State AIDS Control Societies of
NACO in collaboration with the Departments of Education in secondary and senior secondary
schools to build up life skills of adolescents to cope with the physical and psychological changes
associated with growing up and to enable them to protect themselves from HIV/AIDS/STI. After

8
it was suspended in eight States (Chhattisgarh, Gujarat, Kerala, Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh,
Maharashtra, Rajasthan, and Uttar Pradesh), due to a serious follow up and revision of the toolkit
(Educational Material) in 2008, by NACO, the programme was resumed as part of school health
programme under NRHM or through NGOs in the States of Kerala, Gujarat and Rajasthan. Serious
efforts are on for resumption of the programme in the other five States (Chhattisgarh, Karnataka,
Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, and Uttar Pradesh) where it continues to be suspended.
NACO is continuing its efforts through the State AIDS Control Societies (SACS), in States
where the Adolescence Education Programme, is still under suspension (Chhattisgarh, Karnataka,
Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra and Uttar Pradesh). The SACS in these States are once again being
asked to discuss this issue with the State education departments to look into ways of implementing
the Adolescence Education Programme.
XI. NEW STRATEGIES
Recommendation/Observation
(i) Setting up of District AIDS Prevention and Control Unit (DAPCU)
1.12 The Committee appreciates the efforts being made by the Department to train the staff
posted in different DAPCUs throughout the country. However, it feels that keeping in view the
severity of the disease, there is a pressing need to provide training to more staff in order to ensure
more focus on the preventive aspect of the disease control programme. The Committee emphasizes
that the Department should not only strive to achieve the target fixed but depending on the
requirement and situation may also enhance both financial and physical targets . (Para 11.3)
Action Taken
NACO will ensure refresher training to existing staff and induction training to newly
recruited staff.
Recommendation/Observation
(ii) Scheme of link workers in rural areas of Category A & B Districts
1.13 It may be recalled that in its previous report on the Demands for Grants 2010-11, the
Committee has recommended to increase the reach of the scheme to cover all the states in the
country. However, as per information received from the Department in the context of Demands for
Grants 2012-13, the Department has covered only 209 districts. The Committee, therefore,
reiterates its earlier recommendations that the Department needs to assess the scheme so as to
cover the remaining districts and closely monitor the schemes as the success of this scheme is
crucial for achieving the goal of halting and reversing the epidemic of AIDS. (Para 11.6)
Action Taken
Since inception, the link worker scheme (LWS) has been funded completely by donor
agencies (including GFATM) for implementation in 209 districts across 20 States. Since the
partnership with various Donor Partners have ended on 31st March, 2012, LWS is proposed to be
implemented in 163 Global Fund for AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria (GFATM) supported ‘A and
B’ category and highly vulnerable districts across 18 States from Apr 2012 onwards.
The selection of Districts have been done based on the epidemiological scenario, and the
absence of other specified schemes for addressing the issues related to high risk groups, vulnerable
population and people living with HIV/AIDS. Through these parameters, the Scheme has been able

9
to cover the high prevalent and highly vulnerable Districts of the country where the rural
intervention is most needed.
(iii) Preferred private provider scheme for management of sexual infections among the
high risk groups (HRG)
1.14 The Committee notes that the efforts made by the preferred private providers are successful
in bringing about decline of Sexually Transmitted Infections (STI) prevalence among high risk
group from 11.8% to 8.4% in the first three quarters of 2011-12. However, the Committee feels
that there is a need to speed up management under this scheme as the figure of 8.4% is still on
the higher side and much more efforts need to be undertaken on this front. The Committee would
like to be regularly apprised of the action taken in this regard. The Committee also feels that these
private providers should be trained in the rational prescription of antibiotics as this will address
drug resistance issues in the long run. (Para 11.8)
Action Taken
The matter is noted for compliance. Preferred providers are trained on standardized STI/
RTI treatment. To address emergence of drug resistance the providers are provided with pre
specified colour coded drug kits to treat common STI syndromes apart from training them on
rational usage of antibiotics. The preferred private provider approach is planned to be continued in
NACP-IV . In order to reduce STI prevalence amongst HRG, there would be due emphasis on
ensuring access of the essential STI service package to all HRGs through flexibility in the modality
of service delivery to them.
To further reduce STI prevalence of 8.4% among HRG, it has been planned to scale up STI

CHAPTER-II
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS WHICH THE COMMITTEE DOES
NOT DESIRE TO PURSUE IN VIEW OF THE GOVERNMENT’S REPLIES
I. INTRODUCTION
Recommendation/Observation
2.1 Prima facie , a look at the communicable and non-communicable disease burden profile of
the country suggests there could be more pressing issues which could have been the prioritized
over HIV/AIDS, and yet the Ministry in its wisdom went on to create a separate Department for
it. While the committee understands that HIV/AIDS is a genuine health problem which requires
timely addressal, it fails to understand the reason why the Ministry went on to create a dedicated
Department to take care of the issue. The Committee also appreciates the fact that while resource
constraint is a reality given our circumstances, it, at the same time mandates more prudence while
allocating national priorities. During evidence, the Committee queried the Department to justify this
act, and to the Committee’s dismay no satisfactory answer was provided. Further, a post-evidence
written query was made and the Department forwarded the same to the Ministry to be replied.
Answer to this is still awaited till the compilation of this Report. The Committee takes serious view
of this delay on part of the Ministry as time crunch at the time of DFGs is to be anticipated as
is prompt response.The Committee recommends that the response be communicated to them in
detail at the time of the presentation of the ATN within the stipulated three months from the date
of presentation of this Report in the Parliament. (Para 1.1)
Action Taken
India is a low prevalence country but has the third largest population of HIV infected people
in the world. Even a small percentage increase in prevalence will result in a large number of HIV
infection on account of population size. Though a series of measures, including the organizational
framework at the governmental level i.e. the National AIDS Control Organization (NACO) were in
place, the magnitude of the problem warranted a more focused attention.
2. AIDS related issues were handled by the Department of Health and Family Welfare.
However, the overall ambit of that Department was very large. Therefore, in the then existing set
up, a more focused attention and a multi-dimensional approach was not possible. Moreover, the
gravity of the problem also needed to be gauged by the fact that it affects the population in the
most productive age groups. Similarly, there was a need for coordinated action for a high focused
cutting edge research in this area.
3. In the above context, it was felt necessary to create a separate Department of AIDS Control
to be located within the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare by amending the Government of
India (Allocation of Business) Rules, 1961. This was done to create the necessary space to take
up a whole range of programmes to effectively tackle the problem and provide viable solutions. The
Department was to be oriented exclusively for building an all encompassing response to contain the
spread of this menace by reaching out to the diverse population, dissemination of accurate,
complete and timely information about HIV/AIDS, promotion of measures that are effective for
protection against its spread and provision of free treatment for all those who need it.

12
4. To sum up, Department of AIDS Control was created to provide a sharper focus to
government initiatives in effectively tackling the threat posed by HIV/AIDS in the country. Further,
it was felt that the gravity and magnitude of the problem could be better assessed by a dedicated
Department for the purpose which would spearhead as well as coordinate programmes dealing with
AIDS related issues.
PREVENTION
Recommendation/Observation
2.2 The Committee recommends that treatment should be recognized as a cornerstone of
prevention activities explicitly by Department of AIDS Control. Outcomes of recent scientific
studies show that if an HIV-positive person adheres to an effective antiretroviral therapy regimen,
the risk of transmitting the virus to their uninfected sexual partner can be reduced by 96%. Studies
suggest that antiretroviral therapy reduces the sexual transmission of HIV in generalized epidemics,
especially among sero-discordant couples. There is also growing evidence of the impact of ART
on community-level HIV transmission, both, in generalized and concentrated epidemics including
among injecting drug users. Most importantly the availability of Treatment for Prevention will not
only empower people to get tested for HIV , but also to disclose their HIV status, but significantly
contribute to reducing the stigma and discrimination surrounding HIV . Therefore, it is crucial for
Department of AIDS Control to recognize and use antiretroviral drugs as a prevention tool to
control the epidemic in India. The Committee feels that to capitalize on the scientific evidence,
continued investment in ART treatment is necessary in the coming five years to prevent new
infections. (Para 1.5)
Action Taken
Department of AIDS Control has taken note of a recent scientific study indicating that
treatment with ARV drugs reduces the risk of transmitting the virus to other un-infected sex
partners by 96%. This PHTN 054 study is a multi centric/multi country study conducted at two
sites in India located at NARI, Pune and YRG Care, Chennai. The data from these two sites has
not yet been analysed with specific reference to India. However, the overall preliminary analysis
on this variable at NARI, Pune site, will be done only after the completion of study.
The major concern on this study is that the sites in all other countries are ‘generalised
epidemic’ sites except in India where the epidemic is ‘concentrated epidemic’. The results as
outcome of this study will only be restricted to discordant couples.
The issue of making available treatment for prevention to empower people to get tested for
HIV , which is stated as contributing factor to reduce the stigma and discrimination, was discussed
in the last meeting of the Technical Resource Group (TRG) on ART held in December 2011. The
TRG was of the opinion that the issue of side-effects and emergence of resistance among these
people will be a major deterrent to providing anti-retroviral drugs as prevention tool in our country,
presently. Further, as the high risk populations in the context of HIV are largely divided into two
parts. One, most at risk populations (MARP’s) who are not infected and the other, who are HIV
infected. In the first group ART as prophylactic treatment is currently ruled out in the programme
while for others the ART will be given to those who have CD4 count as < 350.
As a part of planning of NACP – IV, it has been well recognised that providing Care,
Support and Treatment services to PLHIV will be an important component of the programme
during the next five years. Although, Lost to Follow Up (LFU) is presently within acceptable limits,
more efforts will be made to further bring it down during NACP IV.

13
CARE, SUPPORT AND TREATMENT
Recommendation/Observation
2.3 The committee recommends that all persons living with HIV should be offered and
counseled to test for Hepatitis B and Hepatitis C by Department of AIDS Control. As a next step,
clear guidelines, resources and training for the testing of Hepatitis in ICTCs and management of
the Hepatitis co-infection should be provided to ART centers. Costs of Hepatitis drugs alone should
not be a factor to refuse treatment of this co-infection that can cause liver cirrhosis. Efforts to
boost local production of Hepatitis drugs and variety of measures such as bulk Procurement and
health safeguards in the Patent law should be used to reduce prices. (Para 1.6)
Action Taken
The diagnosis and management of Hepatitis B and Hepatitis C to people attending the
hospitals is the mandate of the general health system, as these facilities are to be provided in the
existing health care delivery system.
Thus, Department of AIDS Control may not be asked to duplicate efforts to provide such
facilities in the set up of National AIDS Control Programme. Moreover, a large number of NACO
facilities are located in the same institutions belonging to larger health system like Facility Integrated
Counselling & Testing Centres and ART centres etc.. Whenever a PLHIV attending ART centre is
diagnosed to be co-infected with Hepatitis B and Hepatitis C, he/she is referred to the general health
system for confirmatory diagnosis and management of these diseases.
Recommendation/Observation
2.4 The Committee clearly recommends that Department of AIDS Control strengthen TB
infection control in ART centers to prevent transmission of TB among people living with HIV. The
Committee also clearly recommends that with new tests that can detect DR-TB in less than two
hours, it’s a perfect time for Department of AIDS Control to take immediate action to boost
diagnosis of DR TB in people living with HIV . At ART Centres implementation of intensified TB
case finding (active TB screening) has been abjectly neglected despite clear WHO
recommendations. HIV+ patients often arrive in health facilities in very bad condition and even die
before their DR TB treatment can be diagnosed and appropriate treatment can be started. The
Committee feels that Intensified case finding with access to culture/DST testing can increase
access to early treatment of DR TB for people living with HIV in the public programme with
appropriate drug regimens. Usually people living with HIV have already been treated in the private
sector with inappropriate TB drug regimens. The Committee notes that recent studies in scientific
journals like PLoS have documented that the proliferation of TB formulations in the private market
coupled with the casual over-the-counter sale of antibiotics, of which some are used for DR TB
treatment, is fuelling the development of drug resistance, which is also affecting people living with
HIV . There is an urgent need for Department of AIDS Control to work with RNTCP and the
DCGI’s office for regulatory control of sale and administration of TB Drugs in the private sector
in order to address the growing incidence of severe forms of DR-TB in India. (Para 1.7)
Action Taken
The Department of AIDS Control is providing support to all ART centres for ensuring
infection control measures to be adopted in these facilities including measures to ensure prevention
of transmission of TB among PLHIV . This is regarded as an integral part of HIV-TB activities at
the ART centres.

14
The Intensified TB Case Finding (ICF) activities are being implemented in all Integrated
Counselling and Testing Centres (ICTCs) and ART centres across the country. The diagnosis of TB
among HIV infected people, who attend the ART centres, is done by referring them to designated
TB Diagnostic facilities in the same institution, where the ART centre is located. As the testing
facilities for diagnosis of TB already exists in the same institute, the Deptt. of AIDS Control is not
duplicating the efforts in this regard.
The diagnosis of Drug Resistant TB (DR TB) by newer technologies is the mandate of
Revised National TB Control Programme (RNTCP) being implemented by Central TB Division in
Department of Health. In this regard, there is a Joint National Technical Working Group (NTWG)
for coordination of HIV & TB activities. This group explores and directs both programmes to
initiate such activities in improving the management of HIV/TB co-infection. Similar State level
Committees exist at state level to ensure the proper coordination between the two programmes so
that the activities both at TB clinic and ART centres (HIV/AIDS clinic) are well coordinated for
the benefit of patients with HIV/TB co-infection.
As regards regulatory control of sale and administration of TB drugs in the private sector,
in order to address the growing incidence of severe forms of Drug Resistant TB cases in the
country, it is conveyed that this is the mandate of Drugs Control Authority i.e. Drugs Controller
General (India) and RNTCP. However, this will be taken up by the Department in the next meeting
of NTWG.

III. ROLE OF NGOs
Recommendation/Observation
2.9 The Committee is dismayed to note that the Department has not been able to recover the
unspent balances available with the discontinued NGOs. There appears to be some slackness on the
part of the Department and other implementing agencies. The Committee, therefore, recommends
imposing severe penalties on the NGOs which indulged in fraud or financial embezzlement. If need
be, the Department should sound the law enforcement agencies of the concerned States to proceed
with action against such NGOs as fraud or financial embezzlement comes within the domain of
penal offences requiring expertise and wherewithal of law enforcement agencies. (Para 3.2)
Action Taken
State AIDS Control Societies are responsible for contracting NGOs/CBOs for
implementation of targeted intervention projects through a transparent process of expression of
interest followed by Technical Appraisal Committee doing a desk review and Joint Appraisal
Committee (JAT) doing a field verification of the capacity of NGO before the contracting is
approved by the Governing Body headed by Secretary/Principal Secretary of the State. The
performance of the NGO is monitored and the poor performing NGOs/CBOs are terminated based
on the assessment or independent evaluation process. The first instalments of funds are released
as an advance and the monthly Statement of expenditure (SOEs) are monitored by Computerized
Fund Management System (CPFMS). Before the next instalment is released, the previous SOEs is
settled. This process helps in lowering the outstanding amounts with the NGOs.
State AIDS Control Societies (SACS) have already initiated the above steps to keep a tab
on the expenditure of NGOs and thereby decrease the outstanding amounts with the NGOs without
compromising the field implementation. After the statutory audits, SACS recover the unspent
balance amount from NGOs/CBOs and those NGOs not complying with necessary legal actions are

17
taken by involving the district collector or Commissioner. Out of the total outstanding from NGOs
amounting to Rs. 352.7 lakhs in 27 States, an amount of Rs. 221.5 lakhs has been recovered which
is 63 per cent. NGOs in 14 States have a balance of Rs. 131.08 lakhs still to be recovered. District
administration has been requested to expedite the recovery process. Legal actions have also been
initiated against the NGOs who have not responded to the notice. Legal actions have been initiated
for NGOs in 8 States.
VII. PERSONS TO BE COUNSELLED AND TESTED AT ICTCS (TARGET OF 220 LAKH
PER YEAR)
Recommendation/Observation
2.10 The Committee finds that these are fleeting statements based on assumptions. Street
children for example are sexually active at a very young age. New studies also establish that
assumptions that young people below 15 years are not sexually active are not accurate.
Interventions for young people are necessary to address the risk of STDs, HIV and Hepatitis and
the Committee recommends that the Department make appropriate provision for capturing this risk
group. Another scenario was presented before the officials during oral evidence-a long-haul truck
driver/migrant labour (the two highest risk – groups) contracting infection from a sex-worker and
passing it on to his wife back in the village-chances of the wife thus getting infected and becoming
pregnant and being captured as a new case? The Committee for want of a satisfactory answer
recommends that the Department take a very serious view of this critical gap in data generation
as it feels that given the poor accessibility to health care in rural areas the chances of such cases
being captured in data collection would be truly grim. The Committee feels that citing international
norms and a one-size-fits-all kind of approach is neither adequate nor acceptable while capturing
data in a truly diverse country like India. The Department must come up with more innovative
solutions after consulting the various stakeholders so that a more realistic picture is available for
dealing with the HIV menace. The examples quoted are only illustrative and not exhaustive. The
Committee would like to be kept apprised of the initiatives undertaken by the Department in this
regard. (Para 7.3) (a)
Action Taken
The mathematical models of Estimation Projection Package (EPP)/Spectrum used for HIV
Estimation are developed by WHO/UNAIDS Global Reference Group and are adopted in all
countries across the world. The models are developed based on the best available evidence globally
that inform the assumptions in estimating infections in different age groups. Based on the review
of the available evidence on infections among children below 15 years age, the model works on
the assumption that all the HIV infections in children are resulting from Mother to Child
Transmission. Adequate and valid evidence is not available currently that establishes other routes
of transmission among children. Efforts will be made to generate the required information to inform
assumptions in modeling pertaining to the transmission of HIV among children.
In order to capture the effect of migration on HIV transmission in rural areas, sentinel
sites under HIV Sentinel Surveillance are being set up at primary health centres in rural areas in
heavy out-migration districts. This ensures that the pregnant women from these villages are
captured in the data collection efforts to monitor the HIV epidemic. However, poor utilization of
public health settings in rural areas is still a limitation to HIV Sentinel Surveillance activities.
Besides surveillance, special in-depth studies are also being conducted to study the dynamics of
HIV transmission due to migration and these studies also inform the programme about the ways
to control it.

18
Recommendation/Observation
2.11 The Committee observes that HIV , Hepatitis B, Hepatitis C share common modes of
transmission. The Committee recommends that the technical feasibility of ICTC centres expansion
to test and counsel for hepatitis in a p hased manner should be undertaken immediately. This is
important as many experts feel that there is a significant but under recognized hepatitis-associated
disease burden in this country. Despite that India does not have a Hepatitis disease registry, or
information on the diseases burden. For example, a Professor & Head of Gastroenterology at
AIIMS, has stated that studies reported from various parts of India estimate that about 20 million
Indians are Hepatitis B carriers and about 8 to 10 million may have silent Hepatitis C virus
infection. These individuals do not know that they have these infections and not only are at risk
of transmitting this disease but also cannot access early treatment preventing late stage liver
cirrhosis and liver cancer. (Para 7.3 (b))
Action Taken
The diagnosis and management of Hepatitis B and Hepatitis C to people attending the
hospitals is the mandate of the general health system, as these facilities are provided in the existing
health care delivery system. Thus, Department of AIDS Control may not duplicate efforts to
provide such facilities in the set up of National AIDS Control Programme as such facilities are in
the large number of cases, located in the same institution. Whenever a PLHIV attends an ART
centre and is found to be co-infected with Hepatitis B and Hepatitis C, he/she is referred to the
general health system for confirmatory diagnosis and management of Hepatitis B and Hepatitis C.
VIII. ANTIRETROVIRAL TREATMENT (ART) CENTRES
Recommendation/Observation
2.12 The Committee feels that it would be in the fitness of things to upgrade the link centres
to ART centres in order to increase the number of patients who can avail treatment as well as
procure drugs near their residence which would go a long way in decreasing the staggering figures
of patients who cannot avail treatment due to inaccessibility of the existing ART centres in the
country. (Para 8.6)
Action Taken
As has been pointed out by the Committee in para 8.5, it is understood that HIV virus is
prone to drug resistance. As ART is a specialised treatment, scale up of facilities to provide ART
is done with caution. NACP stresses proper counselling of patients to ensure complete adherence
to treatment, to prevent drug resistance. As per scheme of Link ART Centres, these centres are
upgraded to ART centres once they have a critical mass of patients for treatment at the centre.
They require adequate infrastructure and other facilities to undertake this specialised care in the
interest of the patients.

Recommendation/Observation
3.2 The Committee notes that against the target of setting up of 39 Blood banks during the
19

Eleventh Plan, only 25 Blood Banks could be set up. When enquired about the reasons for

will be made to have the blood banks functional.
Further Recommendation
3.6 The Committee is dismayed to observe the snail’s pace of progress for setting up the
remaining 14 District Level Blood Banks (DLBBs), out of 39 DLBBs under Phase-III of
NACO. Factual position as given by the Department clearly indicates that majority of the
State Governments have failed to fulfill their commitments of providing infrastructure. The
Committee is of the firm opinion that the difficulties as pointed out by the Department are
not insurmountable and can be taken care of if the matter is pursued vigorously with the
State Governments concerned at the highest level. The Committee, therefore, would like to
impress upon the Department to play a proactive role by taking up the matter with the
concerned State Governments, if need be, at the highest level, and inform the Committee
of the efforts made in this regard and the outcome thereof.
Recommendation/Observation
3.7 The Committee is surprised that in spite of the Committee’s recommendation made in its
42
nd Report on Demands for Grants (2010-11), the Department has moved at a snail’s pace which
is evident from the fact that it has managed only to get the land allotted in November 2011 for
the four metro blood banks. The Committee is dismayed by the callousness on the part of the
Department to disregard its recommendation to have a targeted approach in making the four metro
blood banks functional at the earliest. The Committee expresses its displeasure at this sorry state

21
of affairs and recommends that the Secretary of the Department should take personal interest to
ensure completion of the four Metro Blood Banks at the earliest. (Para 5.7)
Action Taken
3.8 • The Proposal for Setting up of Metro Blood Banks was one of the approved activities
under NACP- Phase III.
• As building and manpower were not part of the proposal, a revised proposal was
submitted to EFC and then to Cabinet for approval.
• Under the scheme, it is envisaged to get the requisite land free of cost by respective
State Governments. However, being all the 4 sites in metro-cities, it was difficult to get
requisite piece of land of this size, that too, in vicinity of medical college hospital.
• The land transfer has been done for sites at Kolkata, Mumbai & Chennai. While for
Delhi site, the same is still pending.
• The DPR 2 for the sites at Chennai, Mumbai and Kolkata was approved by the Steering
Committee on 20.12.2011.
• Revised EFC Memo was circulated on 29.2.2012 and has since been redrafted in view
of revised format issued by Ministry of Finance and due to time and cost overrun a
Standing Committee report has to be enclosed with the Revised Cost Estimate.
• Since the examination of the Department by this august Committee, a Standing
Committee on Time & Cost Overrun, chaired by Secretary, DAC has been constituted.
This committee had two meetings and has submitted its findings on 7.6.2012. The
minutes of the same are under circulation. They will be annexed with the draft RCE for
circulation shortly.
• All efforts are being made by the Department to accelerate the establishment and
functioning of these Metro Blood Banks which will be initiated after all approvals are
obtained.
Further Recommendation
3.5 The Committee is constrained to observe that the Project concerning setting up of
the Metro Blood Banks has been plagued by delays due to faulty planning which is evident
from the fact that building and manpower were not part of the original proposal which
necessitated submission of a revised proposal first to EFC and then to Cabinet and thus
resulted in time and cost overruns. More than two and a half years have passed since the
Committee made recommendations in this regard in its 42nd Report presented to
Parliament on the 28th April, 2010, but the execution of the project still remains a far cry.
The Committee, therefore, urges upon the Department to review the strategies adopted so
far in the implementation of the Project and incorporate necessary modifications in the
same with a view to expedite the project at the earliest.
VII. PERSONS TO BE COUNSELED AND TESTED AT ICTCs (TARGETS OF 220 LAKH
PER YEAR)
Recommendation/Observation
3.10 As per information submitted by the Department, it has set an overall target of 220 lakh

22
people per year (including pregnant women) to be counselled and tested in ICTCs at the end of
NACP III i.e. March, 2012. However, a plain reading of the figures furnished by the Department
reveals that the Department has not been able to achieve its scaled down targets. Further, as per
information furnished by the Department, total approved number of posts of counsellors in ICTCs
is 4992 whereas the actual strength is 4774. Similarly the sanctioned strength of the post of lab
technicians in ICTCs is 4702 whereas the actual strength is 4352. The Committee expresses
displeasure that the Department has not been able to fulfill even its scaled down targets. However,
the Committee supports any endeavour by means of which the Department would be able to
achieve the targets fixed by it. If need be, it would support the Department to seek additional funds
from the Finance Ministry/Planning Commission so as to augment the manpower as well as number
of stand-alone ICTCs with the rider that the Department makes serious efforts to achieve its yearly
targets. (Para 7.2)
Action Taken
3.11 The Department has made efforts to scale up counseling and testing services by
collaborating with NRHM to establish Facility Integrated Counseling and Testing Centres. Workload
of ICTC is continuously reviewed to ensure optimal utilization of available human resource.
The vacancies among counselors and laboratory technicians has been a constant challenge
for the Department due to
(i) inability of some States like Odisha to fill up the vacancies due to court cases and
other administrative issues
(ii) attrition of staff at field level
(iii) overall shortage of qualified laboratory technicians in the States
To address this challenge, wherever there is a vacancy, the department ensured continuity
of counseling and testing services by training the general health system laboratory technician and
utilizing their services.
Further Recommendation
3.12 The Committee is not satisfied with the reply of the Department. The Committee
feels that if the court cases had been pursued vigorously, pronouncement of verdicts could
have been expedited. As regards resolving administrative issues and dealing with attrition
of staff at field level, the Committee is of the firm view that these issues could have been
easily taken care of by streamlining the decision-making process and offering adequate
incentives. The Committee, therefore, would like the Department to show vision in dealing
with such issues and advise the State Governments accordingly, instead of devoting its
energies to quick-fix solutions.
IX. NEW INITIATIVES
(i) SETTING UP OF NATIONAL BLOOD TRANSFUSION AUTHORITY (NBTA)
Recommendation/Observation
3.13 The Committee expresses its dismay over the fact that the Department of Expenditure has
not sent its comments so far. Though the original timeline for starting NBTA was April, 2010, there
is still no ray of hope of its being set up in near future. The Committee condemns such
procrastinating attitude of the government. The Committee impress upon the Department that in
order to ensure setting up of a National Blood Transfusion Authority, it is imperative that immediate

23
steps should be taken to remove the legal infirmities raised by the Ministry of Finance along with
seeking replies from respective Departments without further delay in view of the fact that the
scheme which was to take wings in the Eleventh Plan is yet to take off. (Para 9.2)
Action Taken
Status Note on Establishment of National Blood Transfusion Authority (NBTA)
3.14 • The Proposal for Setting up of NBTA was one of the approved activities under NACP-
Phase III.
• A vision document on NBTA was prepared in 2008 which was reviewed during a
meeting of experts.
• The proposed budget allocation for NBTA was 39.55 crores for 2 years under NACPIII.
• A draft Cabinet note was prepared and sent to various departments such as Dept. of
Expenditure and Economic Affairs, under Ministry of Finance, Dept of Health and
Planning Commission for comments in September 2009
The Ministry of Finance has not supported the proposal and the detailed observations are
as given below:
1. The intent of NBTA and SBTAs, as clarified in the responses of the revised proposal
is facilitation of the regularity functions of the DCI. These functions can be done
through the existing set up of NBTC and SBTCs which were set up for the purpose.
If necessary, these existing entities could be further strengthened.
2. It has been indicated that State Governments spend Rs. 700 Crore on blood banks
annually and the intent is that these funds would be provided to NBTA to enable it
manage these blood banks through the respective SBTAs. Prima facie, it is not clear
why the State Governments would provide these funds to NBTA without a specific legal
provision, or whether alternate/additional central funding is being conceived here. It is
difficult to support the present formulation without a clear understanding of the fund
requirement and its source in the present case.
3. What appears to have been proposed is taking over regulation and administration of
blood banks (including financial administration) by NBTA through SBTAs. Prima facie,
it does not appear to be feasible without a clear legal mandate in this regard.
4. The fund requirement (over 2010-12) for establishing the NBTA and SBTAs has been
reduced and it has been stated that these funds would be made available out of
NACPIII. Even as the source of funding of the new proposed entities has been clarified
there remains a requirement of appraisal of expenditure proposals at the appropriate
forum before considering their approval.
In view of the above, the matter was not pursued further.
Further Recommendation
3.16 While looking into the reasons for non-approval of the proposal, the Committee finds
that the basic premise for non-approval of the same is the legal infirmities existing in the
present scheme and the requirement of appraisal of the expenditure proposals at the
appropriate forum before considering their approval. The Committee, therefore, impresses
upon the Department to have a relook at the scheme based on Finance Ministry’s detailed
observations and try to remove the infirmities and submit the same again for reconsideration
and approval.

24
(ii) SETTING UP OF PLASMA FRACTIONATION CENTRE (PFC)
Recommendation/Observation
3.17 The Committee is disappointed by the snail’s pace to set up Plasma Fractionation Centre
which is still bogged down in bureaucratic red-tapism even though the Eleventh Five Year Plan has
come to an end. The Committee, therefore, impresses upon the Department to make all out efforts
for setting up of Plasma Fractionation Centre without any further delay. (Para 9.4)
Action Taken
• The Proposal for Setting up of Plasma Fractionation Centre was one of the approved
activities under NACP-Phase III.
• The Centre will have the capacity to fractionate 1.5 lakh litres of plasma per annum
collected from all NACO supported blood banks in the country
• The direct benefit of implementation of this project is to ensure access of plasma
derivatives to needy patients at affordable costs. This will also reduce our dependence
on imported products saving the foreign exchange.
• As building and manpower were not part of the proposal, a supplementary proposal was
submitted for approval.
• The total outlay for the scheme is Rs. 250 crores.
Current Status
• Tamil Nadu Government has provided the land for establishing the PFC at New Avadi
Road, Anna Nagar, Chennai measuring approximately 1.5 acres.
Issues of Concern
EOI for the Project Management Consultant selection was published in May, 2010. During
July, 2009 to January, 2011 the blood safety work was placed at Ministry of Health and Family
Welfare as per decision of Hon’ble HFM which has been transferred to Department of AIDS
Control since January, 2011. In this period NACO convened national and international consultations
to arrive at the technology to be used for the PFC plant. As the proposal was prepared with costing
of 2007-08 it is likely that the estimated cost will be escalated which may require a fresh EFC
approval.
Departmental Efforts to remove bottlenecks
A meeting of the expert group was held on 4 th February, 2011 which short listed 5
companies amongst the 14 EOIs received as Project Management Consultant (PMC).
Request for Proposal (RFP) was prepared for onward communication to the selected
companies. No company was found to be suitable for the same and the whole process is being
reworked.
As the country has no expertise in the area of plasma fractionation the project has been
delayed. Further, cartelization of the technology providers in this area is causing concern in
identifying the appropriate technical resources. Further, the cost estimation will be revised as there
has been an escalation in the price since 2007-08.

25
Further Recommendation
3.19 The Committee is dismayed at the manner in which setting up of a Plasma
Fractionation Centre is still entangled in paper work. It shows the lackadaisical approach
of the Department for setting up Plasma Fractionation Centre. Though, the reply of the
Department indicates the progress made so far, the reasons for the delay are not justified.
In the opinion of the Committee, this is a case of poor planning and implementation
strategy on the part of the Department. The Committee, therefore, recommends to the
Department to revisit its strategy and set out necessary time-bound corrective measures to
achieve the target at the earliest.
XVI. HIV/AIDS Bill
Recommendation/Observation
3.20 The Committee expresses its displeasure on inordinate delay in bringing about HIV/AIDS Bill
even though six years have lapsed since it was first drafted in 2006. The reasons given by the
Department are not acceptable and frivolous and clearly indicate the manner in which it continues
to sideline this crucial law that is aimed at not only protecting the rights of people living with HIV
and marginalized population but also to protect public health. The cases of discrimination in
healthcare, education and within their families have not gone down and in fact continue to endanger
the lives of millions of HIV+, while the Department delays action. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that the Department should take urgent measures to speed up the process for
introduction of the bill as soon as possible, keeping in view the nature of the diseases. (Para 14.4)
Action Taken
3.21 The recommendation of the Committee has been noted. As indicated earlier, the draft of the
Bill was recast and referred to Ministry of Law and Justice in September, 2011 and again in
December, 2011 for vetting. Thereafter, a note along with the draft of the Bill was prepared which
was circulated to various Ministries/Departments in March, 2012, for their comments. The
comments of most of the Ministries/Departments have been received which are being examined.
Comments of few are awaited. They have been reminded to expedite their comments. The
Department has been taking all measure to speed up the process for completion of various
requirements before introduction of the Bill in the Parliament.
Further Recommendation
3.22 The Committee understands that the proposed HIV/AIDS Bill requires detailed
analysis before being introduced in the Parliament. At the same time the Committee
expects that the Department could have been more proactive in taking the Bill to its logical
conclusion. The Committee, therefore, urges upon the Department to take concrete steps
to ensure that the Bill is introduced at the earliest.

the Department of Health Research for the year 2012-13.

CHAPTER-I
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH REPLIES
OF THE GOVERNMENT HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE COMMITTEE
BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
Recommendation/Observation
1.1 The Committee notes that in-principle approval of the Planning Commission has already
been obtained for most of the Schemes which could not take off during the Eleventh Plan due
to lack of necessary approvals. The Schemes or sub-components of the Schemes, which have
received Planning Commission’s in-principle approval, include Promotion and Guidance on
Research Governance Issues, Inter-sectoral Coordination in Medical, Biomedical and Health
Research, Advanced Training in Research in Medicine and Health, Matters relating to
Epidemics, Natural Calamities and Development of Tools; Coordination in the field of Health
Research with Governments, Organisations and Institutes; Matters relating to Scientific
Societies and Associations; Charitable and Religious Endowments in Medicine and Health
Research areas etc. The Committee takes note of the submission of the Department of Health
Research that the allocated funds for the year 2012-13 would be able to meet only part of the
cost of the new activities and this resource crunch from the beginning would seriously affect
the goals of Department, especially new activities. The Committee, therefore, views with
serious concern the considerably reduced BE allocation vis-à-vis  projected outlay for 2012-13 .
(Para 2.12)
Action Taken
DHR has planned its schemes as per the projected outlay for the 12th Plan. However, DHR
will initiate its activities within allotted budget for 2012-13 and will request the Finance Division/
Planning Commission to increase the allocation at RE stage. Department will try its best to achieve
the targets depending upon the availability of the funds.
The Department is thankful to the Hon’ble Committee for accepting its submission that the
funds allocated will enable it to only meet a part of the costs of the new activities and for its
concern for the adverse impact this will have on the Department’s goals.
Recommendation/Observations
1.2 Considering the fact that scientific knowledge generated through health and biomedical
research is used to develop drugs, diagnostics, vaccines, and devices that ultimately find place
in the health care delivery systems of the country as also the fact that health research has a

Recommendation/Observation

utilization of funds is of paramount importance. Equally important is the fact that the attention

like the Department to get all on-going research projects, being funded, wholly or partially with
Government money, evaluated by an independent agency and place the findings in the public
domain. (Para 3.26)

As advised, the Department will formulate the strategies for analysing the research outputs
in terms of health outcomes. Currently the final reports of all the projects are evaluated by ‘external
and independent’ Project Review Committees constituted for different subjects. The Department
will take action to put these findings and opinions of the Expert Committees as well as specific
evaluation of health outcome in public domain as recommended by the Standing Committee.
The Department is thankful to the Hon’ble Committee for endorsing its assessment that the
efforts in the domain of health research should be targeted at health outcomes, and benefits
accruing to the common man through more efficient therapeutics, affordable diagnostics and
products.
The Department will implement the recommendation of the Hon’ble Committee to get the
research activities (intramural/extramural), currently being peer reviewed by non-CMR subject
experts, evaluated by an independent agency and place the findings in the public domain.
Recommendation/Observation

greater clarity, the Committee would like to recommend to the Department to introduce the above
achievements into the public health systems of the country at the earliest opportunity. The
Committee would like to be apprised of the progress made in this direction. (Para 3.28)
Action Taken
For the purpose of the assessment of technology/knowledge advancement into public health
care system, the department has already constituted an advisory group for working out the
constitution of Medical Technology Assessment Board. The Board has to be constituted for review
and to make recommendations for inclusion of technology/knowledge advancement in public health
system. The progress of the same will be communicated to the Parliamentary Standing Committee
on Health and Family Welfare. The Department is thankful to the Hon’ble Committee for its
appreciation of ICMR’s achievements.
The progress made in regard to the 30 leads being pursued for conversion into diagnostics
etc., is indicated in the Annexure.

BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
Recommendation/Observation
2.1 The Committee is constrained to observe that there is a huge mismatch to the tune of
Rs. 2379.43 crore between the Eleventh Plan outlay and the Plan allocations made for the
Department of Health Research. The Committee feels that the financial outlay earmarked for the
Eleventh Plan was based more on theoretical anticipation rather than factors like past trends of
expenditure, stages of formulation/implementation of various projects, the status of pre-project
approvals etc. The Committee would, therefore, strongly recommend that all possible measures
should be put in place to exercise greater financial prudence for the purpose of earmarking realistic
outlays for the Twelfth Plan Period. (Para 2.6)
Action Taken
Against the approved plan outlay of Rs.4496.08 crores by the Planning Commission, the
actual allotment of funds to the D/o Health Research amounted to Rs.2116.65 crore and the actual
expenditure was Rs.1933 crores. It would therefore, be observed that utilisation against actual
allocation was 91.30 percent. The minor shortfall was due to the establishment of the department
in the later half of 2007, belated ‘in principle’ approval to the schemes of DHR by the Planning
Commission in December 2010 and non-approval of the two schemes within the Eleventh Plan due
to procedural delays and partial approval of other two schemes by the internal finance division of
the Ministry with their scope reduced to include only the remaining period of Eleventh Plan, that
too only for the last few months of the last year of the Eleventh Plan, i.e. 2011-12.
The Department would follow the financial prudence while drafting its demands for fund
in future. The Twelfth Plan was prepared after detail discussion. The department has taken up the
matter with the Planning Commission for earmarking outlay commensurate with the projects/
schemes of the Department.
Recommendation/Observation
2.2 The Committee understands that the 12th Plan outlay of the Department is yet to be
approved. The Committee observes that the delay in formal approval of the 12th Plan outlay has
a direct bearing on the process of EFC/CCEA approvals of various schemes/programmes of the
Department and their implementation. The Committee observes that the 11th Plan has already
concluded in March, 2012 and the process of approval of the 12th Plan should have been
completed much before so as to obviate procrastination. The Committee, accordingly, recommends
to the Government to quickly complete all the formalities related to planning process and approve
the 12th Plan outlay in right earnest so that the implementation of various schemes/programmes of
the Department is not hampered by lack of approvals. (Para 2.14)

7
Action Taken
DHR has incorporated the recommendations of the Standing Committee while preparing
EFCs of the four schemes for submission to Government. The EECs of the four schemes have
been submitted for appraisal and requisite approvals. The Department has done the ground work
to launch its schemes as soon as the approvals are granted.
The Hon’ble Committee’s concern at the delay in the finalisation of the Departments’ 12th
Plan outlay, and its consequential adverse impact on the schemes/programmes of the Department
has been communicated to the Planning Commission.
Development of Infrastructure for Promotion of Health Research
Recommendation/Observation
2.3 The Committee welcomes the initiatives taken by the Department for establishment of MRUs
and MRHRUs. The Committee observes that while there is clarity about the fact that the
government medical colleges would be given support for development of infrastructure in terms of
establishment of multidisciplinary research units, there is lack of clarity on the policy stance of the
Development about the model ( i.e. government, private or PPP) to be adopted for establishing the
MRHRU. The Committee expects the Department to remove this ambiguity. (Para 4.7)
Action Taken
The Department will like to inform the Hon’ble Committee that in its considered view the
proposed MRHRUs’ are proposed to be set up as a Government activity and not in a PPP mode.
The scheme has been formulated by the Department in two parts provides for (1) establishment
of Multi-Disciplinary Health Research Units (MRUs) in Government Medical Colleges with 100%
financial support by the DHR for period of five years and thereafter, transfer of recurring
expenditure liability to the concerned State Government/Medical Colleges; and (2) establishment of
Model Rural Health Research Unit (MHRUs) to be run as Departmental Units with 100% funding
by the Department of Health Research and the State Governments responsibility will be limited for
providing requisite land.
The MRHRU will drive the research agenda as per local/regional needs so that the
technology is introduced into the States as per their needs on dynamic basis. This aspect has since
been clearly delineated in the proposal for the EFC.
Recommendation/Observation
2.4 The Committee notes that the above initiatives are targeted to bridge the gap in the
availability of infrastructure for research in medical colleges and create infrastructure for transfer
of technology to the beneficiaries in rural areas. From the information furnished by the Department,
the Committee gathers that EFC for this scheme is yet to be approved whereas the Planning
Commission has accorded its in-principle approval to it. For enabling operationalization of the
Scheme at the earliest, the Committee would expect the Department to make vigorous efforts to
get the clearance of EFC at the earliest and obviate further delays. The Committee desires to be
apprised of the steps taken by the Department to get the EFC approval expedited. (Para 4.8)
Action Taken
Department has already started its efforts to get the approval of its scheme in question. The
EFC for the Scheme for Twelfth Plan Period have already been prepared and processed through

8
IFD for circulation amongst the appraisal agencies and obtaining requisite approvals, as per the
prescribed procedure.
Recommendation/Observation
2.5 The Committee apprehends that meagre outlay of Rs. 44 crore would not be sufficient to
meet the requirement of funds under this head, especially in view of the fact that development of
infrastructure is a capital-intensive activity and 60 proposals for establishment of MRUs and
detailed proposals for establishment of MRHRUs from five States have already been received. The
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Planning Commission have a re-look at the allocations
made under the above head and revise it upwardly at RE stage. (Para 4.10)
Action Taken
The Planning Commission has been apprised of the Hon’ble Committee’s concerns about the
adverse effects of the reduced outlay on this capital intensive scheme, and its desire that the outlay
be enhanced at the RE stage.

Recommendation/Observation
2.6 To address this need, the DHR has been advised to set up apex drug testing laboratories
and related regulatory in every state in synergy/ coordination with DCGI and other appropriate
mechanisms. DHR has also been advised to set up a Medical Technology Development Board to
promote development of indigenous medical technologies. (Para 5.5)

The Department will like to assure the Hon’ble Committee that it will endeavour to finalise
the roadmap for establishing drug testing laboratories in consultation with the DCGI and the
Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. The Ministry has already constituted an advisory group for

The Advisory Group constituted to initiate the process of establishing a Medical Technology
Assessment Board (MTAB) has commenced its work (First meeting held on 3rd August, 2012). The

Recommendation/Observation
2.7 The Committee observes that the activities envisaged under this head are of very vital
importance. However, the real challenge would be witnessed in taking them to their logical
conclusion in a time-bound manner. The fact that a number of activities under the above Scheme,
which were targeted to be finalized during 2008-09, but could not be finalised even after lapse of
4 years, is indicative of the challenges ahead. The Committee, would therefore, like the Department
to lay greater emphasis on the completion of the pre-project activities within a specific time-line.
(Para 5.10)
Action Taken
DHR has already initated action to prepare the EFC note for the scheme for the Twelfth Plan

9
period, indicating the time line/project implementation schedule. The Department has initiated its
pre-project activities for its four proposed schemes.
The Department will like to assure the Hon’ble Committee that it will ensure that all the pre-
project activities are completed well in advance so as to ensure the initiation of action immediately
on receipt of the approval of the Scheme.
Human Resource Development for Health Research
Recommendation/Observation
2.8 The Committee is supportive of the Programme and observes that without a strong human
resource development base all other health research programmes would be rendered ineffective. The
Committee therefore, recommends that the resource crunch should not be allowed to come in the
way of implementation of this important Scheme. (Para 6.6)
Action Taken
The Department is thankful to the Hon’ble Committee for its recommendation for enhanced
funding of the Department. The Department on its part will once again like to assure the Hon’ble
Committee of its commitment to pursue health research in a holistic manner in order to achieve
the multiple goals identified by it ranging from augmenting the human resource pool of researchers;

The Department has already prepared the scheme regarding Human Research Development on
Health Research and submitted the same for comments of IFD before circulation to the appraisal
agencies.
The Department has already requested the Planning Commission to increase its allotment so
that sufficient budget is available for its activities.

reeling under acute shortage of manpower as is evident from the fact that there are only

envisaged to be played by the Department of Health Research, this state of affairs is
unacceptable. The Committee is not aware whether the Department had taken up the
matter with the concerned authorities for augmentation of manpower. The Committee,
therefore, recommends to the Department to take up the matter of shortage of manpower
with the authorities concerned so that if may not hinder the working of the Department.
The Committee would like to be apprised of the measures initiated by the Department to
overcome the shortage of manpower and the outcome thereof.

Recommendation/Observation
3.10 The Committee observes that the shortfall between the projected demand and the Budget
Estimate for ICMR for 2012-13 is to the tune of Rs. 1183.00 crore, which is massive by any
standards and is certain to have an adverse bearing on the implementation of various intramural and
extramural research projects of ICMR. Given the excellent track-record of ICMR in utilizing the
budgeted funds, the Committee wonders as to what financial yardstick was applied leading to
substantially reduced allocation of funds in BE 2012-13 vis-à-vis the projected demand. In view of

of the country, the role of ICMR is very crucial in generating new knowledge in frontier areas of

funding to such a large extent, it can have very serious repercussions for generation of new
scientific knowledge and undermine the desired outcomes in health sector. The Committee,
