CHAPTER-I
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH REPLIES
OF THE GOVERNMENT HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE COMMITTEE
I. BUDGETARY PROVISIONS
Recommendations/Observations
1.1 The Department has informed that the expenditure status of the allocated funds under Plan
heads for the Eleventh Plan was as follows:
(Rs. in crore )
Year B E RE Actual Expdt.
2007-08 2985.00 2331.39 2183.83
2008-09 3650.00 3650.00 3008.40
2009-10 4450.00 3825.25 3261.90
2010-11 5560.00 5139.55 4666.04
2011-12 5720.00 4450.00 4101.41
Total – XI Plan 22365.00 19396.19 17221.58
(Para 1.1)
1.2 From a scrutiny of the above Table, the Committee is constrained to observe that there was
substantial and persistent under-utilization of the budgeted funds during the Eleventh Plan. That the
savings occurred under the Plan head underlines the fact that the development activities have been
curtailed. Though the Committee is supportive of the Department’s demand for higher allocation of
funds, it deprecates the Department for failing to optimally utilize its Plan Allocations over the last
five years. The Committee observes that the underutilization of budgeted funds is indicative of slack
monitoring on the part of the Department as well as formulation of the Budget Estimates in a
ritualistic manner without application of proper financial yardsticks. The Committee, accordingly,
impresses upon the Department to pay focused attention to streamlining its monitoring mechanism
and ensure optimal and more efficient deployment and utilization of its financial resources for
smooth execution of its Plan programmes. (Para 1.2)
Action Taken
Noted for compliance.
Recommendations/Observations
1.3 As per the information furnished by the Department the allocation made vis-a-vis actual
expenditure incurred in respect of some of the major Institutions/projects/initiatives of Department
for the last three financial years is as follows: Annexure-I (Para 1.12)
2

3
1.4 From a perusal of the utilization trend of the allocation as given in the Table above, the
Committee infers that the Department has failed to meet broad committed objectives of the Eleventh
Five Year plan. The Committee feels that the Department needs to introspect the reasons for
underutilization of funds practically in all of its major initiatives targeted to be achieved during the
Eleventh Plan period and take appropriate corrective actions accordingly. In addition to dedicated
approach, advance action plans may also be drawn for completion of all the projects in hand within
the targeted timelines. (Para 1.13)
Action Taken
Noted for compliance.
Recommendations/Observations
1.5 The Committee recalls the following recommendations it has made in its 39th Report:–
“The Committee takes note of the fact that the Department has taken measures like for
non-recurring grants, no fresh releases are being authorized unless audited Utilization
Certificate for grant released in the year prior to the last year ( i.e. with a ‘grace period’
of one year) has been received, subject to the condition that the sanction for the earlier
grant does not permit a longer period of utilization. Further, the provisions of the General
Financial Rules, which require that in case of recurring grants, funds for same purpose
beyond 75% of the next year’s provision will not be released unless audited Utilization
Certificate for the grants released in the previous year is received, are being strictly
implemented. Impact of such measures does not seem to be very effective as number of
pending UCs continues to remain very high. Not only this, such a trend also indicates that
schemes are not being implemented as envisaged.”
“The Committee notes that as a further effort to maximize liquidation of UCs, a
communication has been sent by the Secretary (Health) to the Principal Health Secretaries
of all the States. If need be, this exercise needs to be pursued further with higher
authorities.” (Para 1.18)
1.6 The Committee is deeply disturbed that no heed has been paid to the Committee’s above
observations/recommendations, and a large number of UCs are still pending under both the
Centrally Sponsored and Central Sector Schemes. The additional measure taken by the Department
by sending a communication from the Secretary (Health) to the Principal Health Secretaries of all
the States has also been proved to be futile. The Committee, accordingly, recommends that the
Department needs to have a serious introspection of the reasons for pendency of such a large
number of Utilization Certificates and come out with clear and innovative action plans for
liquidation thereof. (Para 1.19)
Action Taken
The Office of CCA has been periodically monitoring the pendency of UCs at the level of
different State Governments, and putting up the status to higher authorities in the Ministry. D.O.
letter has been issued to all the Health Secretaries with details of UCs pending in the States. Many
States like Punjab, Tripura, Goa, Jharkhand, Haryana have already responded with details of the
UCs. A drive to reconcile the pending UCs with Divisions shall be undertaken during this quarter.
A monitoring system has also been introduced on the website of CCA namely
www.ccahealth@gov.in to monitor the status of UCs.

4
Recommendation/Observation
1.7 The Committee is constrained to note that to a pointed query to the Department in this
regard, the Department has either merely stated that the ATN has been submitted to the Audit or
the ATN is under preparation. The Committee rather desires that details of the Action Taken by the
Department on the Audit paras should have been made available to the Committee. The Committee
also takes note of the fact that action on audit paras dating as far back to years 2008, 2009 are
still under preparation stage. The Committee calls for a speedy action on the observations as
contained in audit paras. The Committee would like to be apprised of the action taken in this
regard. (Para 1.21)
Action Taken
The details of ATN on audit paras are at Annexure-II.
As regards speedy action on the submission of ATN on audit paras, following monitoring
system has been put in place to review the status of pending Action Taken Notes:
1. The Standing Audit Committee has been set up under the Chairmanship of Secretary
(Health) with AS&FA, CCA and concerned Joint Secretary as members to review the
pending ATN regularly.
2. ATN Adalats/Workshops with the representatives of audit are held to review the
pending Action Taken Notes/Disputes.
3. Status of pending Action Taken Notes is also reviewed in the Senior Officers’ Meeting
periodically.
4. The Committee of Secretaries is also reviewing the status of pending Action Taken
Notes.
As a result of above reviews, pendency of Action Taken Notes on audit paras has been
greatly reduced from 72 paras as on 01.04.2009.
II. CENTRAL GOVERNMENT HEALTH SCHEME
Recommendation/Observation
1.8 Despite continuous under utilization of funds during the Eleventh Five Year Plan, there is
enhanced allocation in Plan funds from Rs. 78.00 crore in 2011-12 to Rs. 82.81 crore for 2012-13.
The Committee is given to understand that these enhanced funds are meant for meeting the
expenditure on account of salary and wages, purchase of medicines and all other administrative
expenses incurred by some CGHS cities for which budget is allocated under plan Head only  i.e.
Chandigarh, Bhopal, Bhubaneswar, Guwahati, Shillong, Dehradun, Jabalpur, Ranchi and
Thiruvananthapuram. Further, construction of own CGHS building where plots are already allotted
and opening of already sanctioned dispensaries in Delhi and NCR are also proposed during 2012-13.
The Committee observes that the Department has to undertake lot of ground work in CGHS and
is of the view that for this purpose the targets need to be set, resources to be placed at the
disposal in time and implementing agencies need to be made accountable for accomplishing the set
targets from the very outset. (Para 2.4)
Action Taken
The observation of the Hon’ble Committee to ensure maximum utilisation of funds is
accepted for compliance in the future.

5
Recommendation/Observation
1.9 The Committee notes that the earmarked funds for 2012-13 under the scheme are not in
tune with the projected demand of the Department. From the figures made available to the
Committee it is evident that Rs.600.00 crore have been allocated against projected demand of
Rs.759.08 crore under non Plan Head and Rs.82.81 crore against the projection of Rs.92.17 crore
under Plan head. The Committee is given to understand that this deficit in allocation may adversely
affect procurement of medicines. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department
should try its best to convince the Planning Commission and Ministry of Finance, for enhancement
of allocation at RE stage for procurement of medicines. (Para 2.5)
Action Taken
Every effort is made to secure maximum fund for procurement of medicines. The Hon’ble
Committee’s suggestion is noted for compliance at the RE stage for enhancement of allocation
under the Plan head.
Recommendation/Observation
1.10 On a query regarding the settlement of reimbursement claims of CGHS beneficiaries, the
Committee has been apprised of a number of steps taken by the Department to expedite the process
and as a result thereof the pendency has been brought out significantly to 3075 bills all over the
country. The Committee lauds the efforts made by the Department to bring about a significant
reduction in pendency of reimbursement claims and hopes that the Department would strive to
bring this figure further down with its sincere efforts. The Committee likes the Department to issue
a circular intimating the simplified procedures and for dispelling any misgivings among the
beneficiaries. (Para 2.6)
Action Taken
The Hon’ble Committee has appreciated the efforts made by CGHS for addressing the
issues of Medical Reimbursement Claims (MRC). CGHS will keep on making the requisite efforts
to bring about further improvements in the MRC disposal and also to make the process hassle free
and fast for the beneficiaries. The circular issued in this regard has been placed on the CGHS
website – www.cghs.nic.in.
Recommendation/Observation
1.11 The Department has stated that in order to mitigate the problems faced by the CGHS
beneficiaries in getting their bills reimbursed, there is no need of verification of bills by the treating
doctor and submission of essentiality certificate. Also, specific guidelines for examination of
requests for full reimbursement of claims have also been issued. In addition to this, the
beneficiaries now have the option of submitting the original bills under any health insurance scheme
that they may be subscribing and claim the balance amount from CGHS/Department that shall be
as per CGHS rates and regulations. The Committee observes a lot of ambiguity in process of
reimbursement of bills and the facts that are brought to the notice of the Committee are at
variance. The Committee, therefore, recommends to the Department to issue a fresh circular in this
regard addressing all the misgivings currently prevailing among beneficiaries. (Para 2.7)
Action Taken
The recommendation of the Hon’ble Committee is accepted. CGHS will endeavour to make
the system more effective and hassle free for the beneficiaries.

6
Recommendation/Observation
1.12 The Committee is happy to note that 4,332 beneficiaries have opted for the Preventive
Health Check Up Scheme (PHCU) till 19th March, 2012 since its introduction. 30 beneficiaries per
day are registered in advance-online and undergo a list of identified investigations. Keeping in view
the success of the scheme, the Committee feels that these facilities should be made available at all
the Wellness Centers across the country so that more and more CGHS beneficiaries can avail these
facilities. Secondly, the Committee also suggests to the Department to have a monitoring
mechanism to gauge the performance of Preventive Health Checkup Scheme at regular basis so as
to maintain the quality standards of diagnostics and treatment procedures. While appreciating
Department’s efforts to spread awareness about this scheme, the Committee would like to suggest
that Department should publicize it through audio-video aids; newspapers in regional languages, etc.
in order to expand the scheme to a wide range. Also the Department should make efforts to ensure
that CGHS beneficiaries should understand the importance of Preventive Health Checkup Scheme
and opt for it. (Para 2.10)
Action Taken
The Hon’ble Committee’s suggestions are noted. The Preventive Health Check-up scheme
has already been implemented in 8 Wellness Centres in Delhi. It is working well and adequate
publicity is being given to this scheme among the beneficiaries. The initiative has been widely
appreciated. CGHS is contemplating introduction of this scheme in some other places also in a
phased manner.
The scheme is being given wide publicity through posters at the Wellness centre level. The
OM issued in this respect has been placed on CGHS website for public viewing and it has also
been circulated to all Ministries/Departments/Offices of Government of India with request to give
it wide publicity among the beneficiaries. A circular has also been issued in this regard requesting
the CGHS doctors and officials at Wellness centre level to give the scheme wide publicity and
inform and educate the beneficiaries about the importance of preventive health checkup and
motivate them to undergo the preventive health checkup to ensure timely detection and cure of any
disease conditions.
Recommendation/Observation
1.13 In context of Health Insurance Scheme, the Committee is given to understand that as per
the directions of the Committee of Secretaries (CoS), a proposal for inclusion of the Health
Insurance Scheme in the Twelfth Five Year Plan has been sent for consideration of the Steering
Committee of the Planning Commission. This Scheme will require a Plan outlay of approx
Rs.2,600.00 crore over the plan period of five years. After obtaining a go ahead from the Planning
Commission, the proposal would be placed before the Expenditure Finance Committee (EFC) and
finally before the Cabinet for its approval of the Health Insurance Scheme. Request For Proposal
(RFP) for the Scheme will be issued after getting all the requisite approvals. The Committee was
informed that the proposed scheme is mainly for non-CGHS areas and is not a substitute of CGHS.
The Committee appreciates that the above scheme is primarily for non-CGHS areas and is of the
firm view that if at all it is implemented, it should be over and above CGHS facility instead of
replacing it. (Para 2.12)
Action Taken
The proposed Health Insurance Scheme will not be a substitute for CGHS. It is being
contemplated with special focus on non-CGHS areas where the pensioners are not getting adequate
healthcare cover.

7
Recommendation/Observation
1.14 The Committee was informed that around 485 hospitals and 138 Diagnostic centres are
empanelled under the scheme. As far as rates are concerned, the Committee was informed that only
L1 rates are notified & all those hospitals who agree for the notified rates get CGHS approval. The
Committee is constrained to note that the reluctance of the private hospitals and diagnostic centres
for empanelment is because of the low rates quoted by the CGHS for the specialized treatment and
diagnostic procedures due to which the CGHS beneficiaries are deprived of highly specialized
medical care and diagnostic facilities. The Committee hopes that the Department would rationalize
the new package rates as committed in the meeting. (Para 2.20)
Action Taken
The Hon’ble Committee’s observations are noted for compliance.
Recommendation/Observation
1.15 One must not forget that the main objective of CGHS is to provide quality healthcare at
economical rates to the targeted beneficiaries. The Committee, therefore, is of the view that the
rates should be rationalized so that the beneficiaries should be able to avail high quality diagnostics,
laboratories, specialized medical and surgical treatment in various private super specialty hospitals.
The Committee, accordingly, recommends framing of a policy for revision of rates after every two
years to realistically fix the rates of treatment as stated in 39th Report of the Committee on
Demand for Grants 2010-11 and would like to be updated about the action taken by the Department
in this regard. (Para 2.21)
Action Taken

XV. NATIONAL MENTAL HEALTH PROGRAMME
Recommendation/Observation
1.37 The Committee is shocked to see the mismatch between requirement of manpower under

Mental Health Survey and parameters on the basis of which such surveys are carried out by the
Department. (Para 15.7)

16
Action Taken
It is admitted that there is an acute shortage of qualified professionals in the field of Mental
Health in the country which is also a major constraint in meeting the mental health needs and
providing optimal mental health services to the people. Due to shortage of manpower in mental
health, the implementation of the District Mental Health Programme in the country suffered
adversely in previous plan periods. To address the acute shortage of manpower in the field of
mental health, the Department started the Manpower Development Schemes under the National
Mental Health Programme. The scheme envisaged establishment of 11 Centres of Excellence in
Mental Health across the country and strengthening/establishment of 120 PG Departments in Mental
Health Specialties (30 each in Psychiatry, Clinical Psychology, Psychiatric Social Work and
Psychiatric Nursing).
Once fully operational, the Institutes funded under Manpower Development Schemes would
produce 1756 qualified professionals in the field of Mental Health every year as per details at
Annexure-IV .

taken to further enhance the output capacity of the institutes in the future which will further
enhance the rate at which the gap would be bridged. The Ministry is planning to conduct a nation-
wide survey in the current year to assess the current situation of mental health resources in the

by Technical Sub-Committee which truly reflect no-preparedness on the part of the Department.
The Committee, therefore, recommends the Department should even in the absence of any major
disaster, acquire all necessary equipments and create the required infrastructure in order to get it
fully equipped to face any disaster instead of waiting for the disaster to happen and then move
forward for getting prepared to face the same. Almost cent percent under utilisation of allocated
funds indicates lack of seriousness and lacklustre approach on the part of the Department for any
eventuality. (Para 18.2)
Action Taken
The proposed 100 bed Mobile Hospital is state of art, all weather, selfcontained mobile
hospital designed to provide secondary/tertiary level medical, surgical and critical care at or near
disaster site. It can be airlifted or mobilized through rail or road. It is a full-fledged hospital with
support systems including diagnostic and imaging facilities, kitchen, sanitation, water treatment
plant etc. Laying down specifications for over hundreds of equipments, instruments and
customizing it to Indian conditions, took time. Now that the specifications have been finalized, the
procurement would be expedited to follow the guidance given by the Committee. However, this
would require engaging specialized agencies with expertise in international bidding, having know
how of such systems, evaluation and pre-dispatch inspection, installation and commissioning.
Mobile hospital is a component of a broader plan for disaster preparedness in health sector.
All pre-project activities have been completed and the implementation is under process.
Recommendation/Observation

XXI. NA TIONAL TOBACCO CONTROL PROGRAMME
Recommendation/Observation
2.17 The Committee notes with regret that the allocations made at BE stage was reduced
drastically at RE stage during the entire Eleventh Plan period except the year 2008-09. The
Committee fails to comprehend the reasons for same. However, the Department could optimally

should make all out efforts to utilize entire allocations made at BE stage for the year 2012-13.
(Para 21.3)
Action Taken
The allocations made at BE stage have been reduced at RE stage mainly on account of the
fact that the tobacco product testing laboratories could not be set up during the Eleventh Plan due
to various issues such as approval for manpower, procurement of machinery, trainings for staff
and accreditation from NABL for tobacco testing etc. These issues have now been sorted out and
it is expected that the tobacco testing labs will be set up in 2012-13.
Further, some of the States did not furnish the Utilization Certificates and Statements of
Expenditure, due to which further release of the Grants-in-Aid could not be made to them every
year.

30
The Ministry agrees with the view of the Committee that more needs to be done to
eliminate the scourge of tobacco related disease. The Ministry has plans to upscale the programme
in the Twelfth Plan with coverage of all States and districts in phases. The Ministry is also looking
at improvement of the programme components, and its integration to the national programmes on
prevention and control of non-communicable diseases (NCDs) so as to have better outcomes and
synergy, since tobacco is the biggest risk factor for NCDs. The Ministry is also taking up various
other activities in this regard such as issue of guidelines, taking up the implementation of ban on
Gutka with the States, notification of new pictorial health warnings on smoking forms of tobacco,
setting up a national tobacco quitline with a toll free number, changes in the reporting format and
introduction of web-based reporting and feedback system to improve monitoring, visits to States
and districts to follow up implementation of NTCP and compliance with COTPA 2003 at the State/
district level, capacity building through regional workshops and trainings, advocacy workshops with
policy makers and law enforcers etc. at the State level, conducting national review workshop,
strengthening of anti-tobacco helpline through introduction of a webbased reporting system for
registration of complaints against violations of antitobacco law and their dissemination to the state
and district focal points, sustained media and outdoor campaigns with a strategic media plan,
Interministerial consultations for implementation of WHO FCTC guidelines (under Articles 17 and 18)
and the draft treaty on illicit trade in tobacco products (under Article 15).
Recommendation/Observation
2.18 The Committee had commented in its previous reports on the issue of the setting up of
National Tobacco Regulatory Authority and Tobacco Testing Labs. As per the information supplied
by the Department, the former is still at discussion stage while there has been some progress made
regarding the latter. The Committee, while appreciating the efforts made by the Department on the
issue of setting up of Tobacco Testing Laboratories, expresses its displeasure at the laggard
approach taken by Department on the matter of setting up of National Tobacco Regulatory
Authority (NTRA). The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should prepare a
blueprint by the time the said authority would be set up and keep the Committee regularly updated
of the progress made in this regard. (Para 21.4)
Action Taken
Currently three models for setting up NTRA are under discussion:
MODEL-I: The NTRA may be established through a notification under the provisions of
Section 25 read with Section 31(1) of Cigarette and Tobacco Products (Prohibition of
Advertisement and Regulation of Trade and Commerce, Production, Supply and Distribution) Act
(COTPA), 2003. However, NTRA formed through this process will be non-statutory.
MODEL-II: The NTRA may be established through an Act of Parliament by amending the
COTPA, wherein provisions of State level authorities; quasijudicial action; penalty provisions,
speedy trials by Special Courts etc. may be incorporated.
MODEL-III: A hybrid model wherein the NTRA may be notified through Rules issued
under COTPA, and steps may be initiated for establishing a statutory body through amendment to
COTPA 2003.
It is felt that instead of creating a new body, the existing infrastructure of the Food Safety
Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) could be used for the purpose, which can perform the
functions envisioned under NTRA. The rationale for this stand was that creation of a separate
infrastructure for NTRA would be a time taking process, and hence the most feasible option would
be to create NTRA as a sub-ordinate structure/office under FSSAI. However FSSAI has conveyed

31
its reservations saying that not all tobacco products listed in the Schedule to COTPA 2003 can be
classified as food products as per definitions under the Food Safety Standards Act 2006, and hence
NTRA cannot qualify to be a part of FSSAI. The matter is under further discussion with FSSAI
and within the Ministry to take a final view in the matter

I. BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
Recommendation/Observation
3.1 The Committee observes that a shortfall in allocation of funds to the tune of Rs.10507.53
crore vis-à-vis the proposed outlay for 2012-13 that too at a time when the Government has
committed itself to raising its expenditure on health from roughly 1% of the GDP to 2.5% of the
GDP by the end of Twelfth Plan is baffling, to say the least. The public expenditure on health in
the country is one of the lowest in the world and total plan expenditure would need to rise
substantially and consistently before the target expenditure level of 2.5% of GDP is achieved. The
Committee, therefore, desires to know the reasons behind the substantially reduced allocation for
2012-13. The Committee also desires to know the rate at which the total Plan expenditure would
need to grow annually, in order to meet the expenditure level of 2.5% of GDP by the end of the
Twelfth Plan and what would be the share of the Centre and the States therein. The Committee,
therefore, recommends that the Department should make all out efforts to convince the Planning
Commission and the Department of Expenditure for enhancing the annual Plan allocation for the
remaining four years of the Twelfth Plan and also at RE 2012-13 in such a way that the target
of meeting expenditure level of 2.5% of GDP could be achieved. (Para 1.6)
Action Taken
3.2 The approach paper to Twelfth Five Year Plan envisages an increase in total public health
expenditure to 2.5% of GDP by the end of Twelfth Plan. The outlay of both Centre and States
on health would need to be enhanced progressively to achieve the target of 2.5% of GDP. The
States account for approximately two-thirds of the total expenditure. Frontloading of financing of
activities envisaged for Twelfth Plan would be needed for meeting the timelines for the achievement
of target. Department is engaging with Planning Commission to approve the outlay as proposed by
this Department for the Twelfth Five Year Plan and enhance the annual plan allocation for the
remaining four years of the Twelfth Plan. The Committee’s recommendations that Department
should make all out efforts to convince Department of Expenditure for enhancing allocation at RE
2012-13 has been noted for compliance.
Further recommendation
3.3 The Department had been asked to address two pointed queries regarding the
reasons for reduced allocation for 2012-13 and the required rate of increase in Total Plan
allocation to meet the expenditure level of 2.5 per cent of GDP. However, the Committee
is constrained to note that the Department reply is evasive in as much as it fails to shed
light on these queries. The Committee would like the Department to exercise greater care
and precautions while framing its reply in future and also furnish the requisite
information.
33

34
Recommendation/Observation

programmes/heads which are likely to be affected due to substantially less allocation of funds
include PMSSY , Financial Assistance for Strengthening and Upgradation of Medical Colleges,

Committee was informed that NPCDCS was launched in 2010 in 100 districts across 21 States.

Action Taken
Under the National Rural Health Mission, the following steps are being taken to ensure the
reduction in Maternal Mortality Ratio (MMR), Infant Mortality Ratio (IMR) and Total Fertility Rate
(TFR) and improve the health status of children across all the States of the country:
Strategies Adopted for achieving target set for MMR
• For accelerating the pace of reduction in MMR, GoI has identified delivery points
throughout the country based on a minimum benchmark and in the PIP for the year
2012-13 funds are being given to the States for strengthening these delivery points for
improving service delivery.
• States have also been asked to monitor the performance of identified delivery points to
improve its working.
• Name Based web enabled tracking of pregnant women and children under the Mother
& Child Tracking System (MCTS) has been started to ensure and monitor full services
to them.
• A Joint MCP Card of Ministry of Health & Family Welfare (MoHFW) and Ministry of
Women and Child Development (MoWCD) has been launched to provide a tool for
monitoring services for MCH including ANC, INC & PNC and Nutrition interventions
being implemented by both Ministries.
• The Government of India has taken a policy decision to review every maternal death
both at the health facilities and in the community. The purpose of the review is to
identify causes of maternal deaths and the gaps in service delivery for taking corrective
action and not for taking punitive action against service providers.
• Janani Shishu Suraksha Karyakaram (JSSK): A new initiative namely JSSK has been
launched, which entitles all pregnant women delivering in public health institutions to
absolutely free and no expense delivery including Caesarean section. The initiative
stipulates free drugs, diagnostics, blood and diet, besides free transport from home to
institution, in-between facilities in case of a referral and drop back home.
Strategies Adopted for achieving target set for IMR
• Promotion of Institutional Delivery through Janani Suraksha Yojana (JSY): Promoting
Institutional delivery by skilled birth attendant is a key to reducing both maternal and
neo-natal mortality.
• Janani Shishu Suraksha Karyakaram (JSSK): A new initiative namely Janani Shishu
Suraksha Karyakaram has been launched, which entitles all sick newborns being
delivered in public health institutions to absolutely free and no expense for treatment till
30 days after birth. The initiative stipulates free drugs, diagnostics, blood and diet,
besides free transport from home to institution, in-between facilities in case of a referral
and drop back home.
• Sick Newborn such as Special New Born Care Units (SNCUs), New Born Stabilization
Units (NBSUs) and New Born Baby Corners (NBCCs) at different levels are being set
up at different levels to reduce Child Mortality.
• Home based newborn care (HBNC) through ASHAs has been initiated to improve new
born practices at the community level and early detection and referral of sick new born

60
babies through series of home visits. In case of institutional deliveries six visits on days
3, 7, 14, 21, 28 & 42nd days and one additional visit within 24 hours of delivery in
case of home deliveries. Additional visits will be made for babies who are pre-term, low
birth weight or ill. ASHA is being paid Rs. 250 for conducting home visits for the care
of the newborn.
• Mother and Child Tracking System: A name based Mother and Child Tracking System
has been put in place which is web based to ensure registration and tracking of all
pregnant women and new born babies so that provision of regular and complete services
to them can be ensured.
• Capacity building of health care providers: Various trainings are being conducted under
NRHM to train doctors, nurses and ANM for early diagnosis and case management of
common ailments of children and care of mother during pregnancy and delivery. These
trainings are on IMNCI, NSSK, SBA, LSAS, EMOC, BMOC etc.
• Management of Malnutrition: 657 Nutritional Rehabilitation Centres have been established
for management of severe acute malnutrition cases.
• Appropriate infant and young child feeding practices are being promoted in convergence
with Ministry of Woman and Child Development. Village Health and Nutrition Days
(VHNDs) are organized for imparting nutritional counselling to mothers and to improve
child care practices.
• Universal Immunization Programme: Vaccination protects children against many life
threatening diseases such as Tuberculosis, Diphtheria, Pertussis, Polio, Tetanus,
Hepatitis B and Measles. Infants are thus immunized against seven vaccine preventable
diseases every year. The Government of India supports the vaccine programme by
supply of vaccines and syringes, Cold chain equipments and provision of operational
costs.
Strategies Adopted for achieving target set for TFR
• Emphasising more on spacing methods like IUCD.
• Promoting Post-partum Family Planning services especially PPIUCD.
• Increasing the basket of choices.
• Leveraging huge workforce of ASHAs for delivering contraceptives at doorstep as well
as counselling couples for ensuring delay in first child birth and having spacing between
first and second child.
• Ensuring availability of fixed Day family planning services at all facilities.
• Ensuring quality care in Family Planning services by establishing Quality Assurance
Committees at State and District levels.
• Accreditation of more private/NGO facilities for family planning services under PPP.
Increasing male participation and promoting Non-scalpel vasectomy.

VI. NATIONAL VECTOR BORNE DISEASE CONTROL PROGRAMME (NVBDCP)
Recommendation/Observation
1.21 The Department had informed that against a Plan Allocation of Rs.430 crore for 2011-12,
the expenditure was Rs. 412.66 crore till 23.03.12. Further, the target of bringing the number of
cases to less than 1 per 10,000 populations could not be achieved by 2010 as envisaged by
National Health Policy (2002), for elimination of Kala Azar. However, the target is set to be
achieved by 2015. The Department has been allocated at outlay of Rs. 447.00 crore for the year
2012-13. The Committee is at pains to understand that a period of 10 years was not enough to
eliminate Kala Azar and the target date has been further set back by three years. The Committee
feels that the initiatives taken earlier for Kala-Azar elimination did not have the desired impact. The
Committee would, therefore, like to be enlightened about the short-comings identified in the Kala
Azar elimination programme and how the Department plans to re-orient its policies for achieving
the desired results in terms of elimination of Kala-Azar. The Committee also desires that an
evaluation of the implementation of the programme may be undertaken. (Para 6.3)
Action Taken
• Against plan allocation of Rs.430 crore (excluding NE) for 2011-12, the expenditure is
Rs.433.19 crore (excluding NE) till 31.03.12.
• During 2012-13, the plan allocation of Rs.455.73 crore (excluding NE) has been made.
• The target of Kala-Azar elimination (number of cases less than 1 per 10,000 population
at block level) could not be achieved by 2010. However, target data is revised to 2015.
The constraints and shortcomings identified in the Kala-Azar Elimination Programme for
such a delay and revising the target date are as under:
• Till 2008, diagnosis of kala-azar was being done by bone marrow aspiration or
splenic puncture which was possible at District hospital. This used to delay
institution of treatment and allowing transmission to continue.
• Injectable Sodium Stibo Gluconate (SSG) was the drug of choice for treatment of
kala-Azar cases till 2008 and needed hospitalization for institution of treatment.
Moreover, long duration of treatment (one month) lead to non-compliance and non-
responsiveness to SSG.
• Social mobilization for the control of kala-Azar including for indoor residual spray
had been limited and inadequate attention has been paid to behaviour change
communication.
• Because of administrative delays often funds were not received at the District/PHC
level due to non-release of funds. Non-submission of SOE & UCs by the States
hampered release of funds by the Government of India.
• The suggestion of the Committee to undertake an evaluation of the implementation
of the programme has been acted upon by the Department and a meeting of central
panel of experts has been held to finalize the methodology for the same.
Department proposes following initiatives to be undertaken during Twelfth Five year Plan
Period:

63
Surveillance and Case Management
• Strengthening of early case detection and complete treatment:
• Upscaling the use of rapid diagnostic test kits at the PHC level.
• Treatment with new oral drug Miltefosine which has been expanded to all the Kala-Azar
endemic Districts as first line treatment on Directly Observed Treatment (DOT) pattern
as a supervised treatment with patient coding system for tracking.
• ASHAs would be trained and fully involved to ensure complete treatment compliance
with incentive of Rs. 200/- per case.
• Incentive to the patient towards compensation for loss of wages for 28-30 days @ Rs.
50/- per day during the period of treatment.
• Active case detection by increasing the frequency of door to door visit by observing
Kala-Azar fortnight twice in a year and also through camp approach and also to
intensify the searches for PKDL cases.
• Monitoring of diagnosis and treatment will be accelerated by frequent visits by
programme personnel as well as by proposed coordinators.
• Additional human resource, their capacity building and intensive IEC/BCC.
Vector Management
• Indoor residual spraying (IRS) for interruption of transmission will be taken up in all
the 52 endemic Districts of the country to ensure good quality spray and coverage
above 80 %.
• Monitoring of the process and impact of indoor residual spraying would be stepped out
through independent studies on the effect of spraying on vector populations and
susceptibility studies.
• Environment sanitation will be given considerable importance in a BCC campaign to
eliminate the breeding sites of the vector species.
Initiatives are underway for the provision of alternative housing sites to the poor and
marginalized population in the Kala-Azar villages, who are the most common victims of disease,
under the Indira Vikas Yojana.

VIII. NA TIONAL LEPROSY ERADICATION PROGRAMME
Recommendation/Observation
1.24 As per information available to the Committee, the following States have shown the highest
number of cases where leprosy has been detected during the last three years i.e. 2008 to 2011
namely Chhattisgarh, Bihar, Maharashtra, Gujarat, Uttar Pradesh and West Bengal. The Committee
is constrained to note that India still accounts for more than 50% of the new leprosy cases
worldwide. The efforts made so far have still not yielded the desired results. The Committee
would, therefore, strongly recommend to the Department to monitor the measures taken so far to
eliminate this disease. (Para 8.4)
Action Taken
Elimination of leprosy i.e. less than one case per 10,000 population was achieved at National
level in Dec., 2005. The prevalence of leprosy has been decreasing in India over the years. From
a level of 42 cases per 100,000 population in 2001-02, it has come down to 7 cases per 100,000
population in 2010-11. However, considering very long incubation period of the disease which could
be from few weeks to 20 years, India will continue to have new leprosy cases for many more
years to come.
Government of India continues to accord high priority to elimination of leprosy within the
overall framework of National Rural Health Mission (NRHM). Leprosy diagnosis and treatment
services have been integrated into general health care system, and village level functionaries like
ASHAs and Anganwadi Workers are involved in bringing leprosy suspects to the health care system
for their detection and proper treatment. The Government of India is advocating a District specific
approach for elimination of leprosy during the Twelfth plan period (2012-17). The special measures
for achieving elimination at District level include improved and early cases detection and case
management through intensified activities like active case finding, IEC/BCC in the community,
capacity building of medical, para-medical, community workers and improved monitoring and
supervision.

VII. NA TIONAL TB CONTROL PROGRAMME
Recommendation/Observation
2.9 With regard to MDR-TB patients the Department has informed that DOTS strategy has
significantly improved case detection and cure rates beyond 72% and 87% respectively. 28
accredited labs have been set up across the country to diagnose Multi Drug Resistant T.B (MDR-
TB) and 15 are under process which shall be completed by March,2013. 6944 patients have been
provided treatment for MDR-TB upto 2011. Further, the Phase-II trials of the new molecule (TMC-
2007) for treating patients with MDR-TB are underway. It is a multi-country study and in India
two centers namely, National Institute of Research in Tuberculosis, Chennai and All India Institute
of Medical Sciences are participating. The analysis is underway and the study results are expected
shortly. The Committee would like to know by when the analysis would be completed and its study
results published since a lot of time has already elapsed since the clinical trials commenced.
(Para 7.3)
Action Taken
1. Johnson & Johnson’s (USA) research subsidiary, TIBOTEC, is managing the clinical
development of TMC 2007.
2. The Phase I trial was completed in South Africa and results published in 2008.
3. Phase II (part A) was done in South Africa and published in 2009. The study results
showed it reduced the time to sputum conversion to negative and TMC eliminated TB
bacteria more quickly and was shown to be safe and well tolerated in the patients.
4. The second stage of the Phase II (part B) was initiated in late 2009 as a multi-national
trial involving patients in South Africa, Peru, Latvia, India, Brazil, Thailand, the
Philippines and Russia. The stage is still on-going and for which the results are likely
to become available by end 2012 or early 2013.
After successful Phase II trials, the drug will enter Phase-III clinical trials (minimum 5
years) before it is available for routine patient care.

V. RCH FLEXIBLE POOL
Recommendation/Observation
3.13 To accelerate the pace of reduction of Maternal Mortality Ratio (MMR) in the country, the
following steps are being undertaken by the Government of India under the National Rural Health
Mission (NRHM), launched in the year 2005, across the country with a special focus on 18 States
with weak public health indicators and infrastructure:

79
• Promotion of institutional deliveries through Janani Suraksha Yojana.
• Capacity building of health care providers in basic and comprehensive obstetric care.
• Operationalisation of Sub-Centres, Primary Health Centres, Community Health Centres
and District Hospitals for providing 24x7 basic and comprehensive obstetric care
services.
• Name Based Tracking of Pregnant Women to ensure antenatal, intranatal and postnatal
care.
• Mother and Child Protection Card in collaboration with the Ministry of Women and
Child Development to monitor service delivery for mothers and children.
• Antenatal, Intranatal and Postnatal care including Iron and Folic Acid supplementation to
pregnant & lactating women for prevention and treatment of anemia.
• Engagement of more than 800,000 Accredited Social Health Activists (ASHAs) to
generate demand and facilitate accessing of health care services by the community.
• Village Health and Nutrition Days in rural areas as an outreach activity, for provision of
maternal and child health services.
• Health and nutrition education to promote dietary diversification, inclusion of iron and
folate rich food as well as food items that promote iron absorption.
• A new initiative namely Janani Shishu Suraksha Karyakram (JSSK) has been launched
on 1st June, 2011, which entitles all pregnant women delivering in public health
institutions to absolutely free and no expense delivery including Caesarean section. The
initiative stipulates free drugs, diagnostics, blood and diet, besides free transport from
home to institution, between facilities in case of a referral and drop back home. Similar
entitlements have been put in place for all sick newborns accessing public health
institutions for treatment till 30 days after birth.
• To provide essential and basic Newborn Care and Resuscitation, Navjaat Shishu
Suraksha Karyakram (NSSK) has been launched to address care at birth issues i.e.
Prevention of Hypothermia, Prevention of Infection, Early initiation of Breast feeding
and Basic Newborn Resuscitation. Newborn care and resuscitation is an important
starting-point for any neonatal program and is required to ensure the best possible start
in life. The objective of this initiative is to have at-least one person trained in Basic
newborn care and resuscitation at every delivery.
• This training is being imparted to Medical officers, Staff nurses and ANMs at CHC/
FRUs, 24x7 PHCs and Sub-centers where deliveries are taking place.
• The training is for 2 days and is expected to reduce neonatal mortality significantly in
the country.
• As on date more than 66,900 health personnel have been trained in NSSK across the
country.

VII. NA TIONAL T.B. CONTROL PROGRAMME
Recommendations/Observations
3.25 The Committee observes that the fact that India accounts for a fifth of the global TB
burden is indicative of the magnitude of the problem and reminds of the challenges ahead. Though
DOTS (Directly Observed Short Treatment Course) has been found to be highly efficacious, the
Committee believes that the TB patients being treated in the private sector which is largely
unregulated, go unmonitored and there is no regulatory mechanism in place to ensure that the well-
established and validated treatment regimen is followed there. The Committee would, therefore, like
the Department to pay attention to this aspect while formulating its strategies for the Twelfth Plan.
The Committee also desires to be apprised if any assessment has been made regarding cases of
default in treatment of TB. (Para 7.4)
Action Taken
3.26 The point regarding TB patients being treated in the private sector which is largely
unregulated, go unmonitored and there is no regulatory mechanism in place to ensure that the well-
established and validated treatment regimen is followed there and that this aspect be paid attention
to by the RNTCP while formulating its strategies for the Twelfth Plan is noted. Further,
Government has recently issued a notification for mandating all private institutions to report any
TB cases to the district authorities.
3.27 Regarding default in treatment of TB there is an inbuilt routine surveillance mechanism to
assess the default among the TB patients under the Revised National Tuberculosis Control
Programme. Studies have also been conducted under the programme to assess the factors
associated with default. These are then closely monitored through the mechanism of supervision &
monitoring. The default rate under the programme has declined from 6.9% in 2006 to 5.5% in 2011
amongst the New Smear Positive TB patients.
Further Recommendation
3.28 The Committee notes that the default rate under the programme has declined from
6.9% in 2006 to 5.5% in 2011. The Committee expresses displeasure with the mere decline
of only 1.4% in the 5 year period mentioned above. The Committee feels that T.B being
a highly contagious disease, reduction of just 1.4% over a period of 5 years is not sufficient.
The Committee feels that the Department ought to take more stringent steps to increase
the tempo of curative as well as preventive aspects under the programme; otherwise all
measures taken so far would fall by wayside.

sustained without the participation of the Central Pharma PSUs. The Committee is,
however, aware that the revival of Indian Drugs and Pharmaceuticals company which had
been declared sick in 1992 by Board of Industrial and Financial Reconstruction (BIFR) and
is still hanging fire. Besides, the production and sales turnover of Karnataka Antibiotics and
Pharmaceuticals Limited and Rajasthan Drugs and Pharmaceuticals are more or less static
in value terms since 2007-08. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry of
Health and Family Welfare should urgently take up the matter of revival/ modernisation of
all Central Pharma with the nodal Department ( i.e. Department of Pharmaceuticals) so that
the objective of access to quality generic medicines could be realised within the shortest
possible time. The Committee would also like to be apprised of the progress made towards
finalisation of the new initiative, namely “Free medicines for all through Public Health
Facilities”. (Para 16.7)
XVII. V ACCINE MANUFACTURING UNITS
The Committee expresses its displeasure over the slow pace of the revival of the
three vaccine units and feels that the Department is not pursuing the matter vigorously
which has very serious implications on the vaccine prices and the resultant impact on
Universal Immunisation Programme. The Committee, therefore, exhorts the Department to
shed its casual attitude and ensure that the work regarding upgradation of these vaccine
manufacturing units be completed at the earliest. (Para 17.3)
The Committee observes that the Department has not addressed its concern
regarding under-utilisation of funds allocated for CRI, Kasauli in a satisfactory manner. In
a resource constrained country like India, optimal and judicious utilisation of allocated
funds is of paramount importance. The Committee would expect the Department to apprise
it of the roadmap for better financial performance under this head. (Para 17.9)
XXII. TELEMEDICINE
The Committee notes that the Scheme was approved by SFC in December, 2010/
January, 2011. Two years have elapsed since then, but the matter is still under examination.
The Committee, accordingly, recommends the Department to quickly finalise the issues
involved and implement the project at the earliest. (Para 22.3)
XXV. HUMAN RESOURCE FOR HEALTH
The Committee had presented its 60th Report on the NCHRH Bill, 2011 to both the
Houses of Parliament in the Winter Session of the Parliament (December, 2011). While
the Committee expects that the Government has taken into account the
recommendations, nevertheless for the sake of clarity it recommends that while
redrafting the said Bill special emphasis on restoring the autonomy of the existing
Councils; setting up of other Councils; inclusion of AYUSH; adequate participation of
State Governments, etc. be made. (Para 25.4)

89
PART-B
NRHM
I. BUDGETARY PROVISIONS
The Committee notes that the gap between the expected targets and the
achievements are too wide to be comfortable within the first phase of NRHM (2005-2012).
In response to the Committee recommendation to the Department to undertake a review
of NRHM and to take concrete and concerted efforts to plug the gaps and bottlenecks in
the implementation of programme that existed in the first phase, the Ministry has stated
generically that the Ministry has taken note of the above recommendations of the
Committee for compliance, without spelling out the mechanisms envisaged to be employed
to identify the inadequacies and iron them out. The Committee again impresses upon the
Ministry to undertake a thorough review before the second phase (2012-13) is implemented
on the ground and take corrective measures accordingly. (Para 2.5)
The Committee notes the observations of the Planning Commission on the
recommendations of the Committee. The Committee feels that the observation of the
Planning Commission on the absorptive capacity of the State Health Systems require
attention of the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. The Committee feels that
increasing the public spending on health from 1% to 2.5% of GDP by the end of 12th Plan
is a sin-qua-non  for the success of the NRHM flagship scheme. However, the same cannot
be achieved without strengthening the absorptive capacity of State Health Systems. Ministry
of Health and Family Welfare should playa vital role in augmenting the absorption capacity
of State Health Systems. The Committee, therefore, impresses upon the Department to
seriously set its sights on strengthening of the State Health Systems in order to ensure that
the funds released for health systems are capable of being absorbed properly by the State
Health Systems. (Para 2.6 & 2.7)
III. INFRASTRUCTURE STRENGTHENING
HEALTH CARE UNITS
While making the above recommendations, the Committee had expected the
Department to indicate its reaction to desirability or otherwise of contractual appointments
and their impact on offering quality healthcare services and formulate appropriate policy
response accordingly. The Committee is, however, constrained to note that the Department
has sought to wash its hands off the matter by merely stating that the vacancies are filled
up by State/UT Governments and the matter is being taken up with them. Since the
Ministry of Health and Family Welfare is the principal financier of NRHM, it is its
obligation to see that the quality of healthcare services is not compromised in any way and
help the States devise appropriate strategies for the purpose.
The Committee notes from a perusal of the statement (as on 31st December, 2011)
of staff appointed under NRHM on contractual basis across the country that the number of
contractual staff are still substantial as they may not be amenable to punctuality, discipline,
and control. The Committee would also like to be enlightened on the total number of in-
position posts vis-a-vis  sanctioned strength as per RHS 2011 and the measures taken/
contemplated to be taken to overcome the deficiencies as pointed out in RHS 2011.
(Para 3.3 & 3.4)

90
V. RCH FLEXIBLE POOL
The Committee had directed the Department to put in place a rigorous monitoring
mechanism of evaluation of the effectiveness of the measures so taken. However, the reply
of the Department is silent on this aspect. The Committee, therefore, reiterates its
recommendation made in its 54th Report to provide details of monitoring mechanism of
evaluation of the effectiveness of the measures so taken in this regard. (Para 5.3)
JANANI SURAKSHA YOJANA
The Committee is aware that the Expert Group submitted its Report on the
evaluation of the Janani Suraksha Yojana (JSY). A considerable period of time has elapsed
since then. By now the Ministry must have initiated follow-up action on the
recommendations contained in the said Report. The Committee is therefore unhappy to note
that the Department instead of acquainting the Committee with the follow-up action taken
on the findings of the Expert Group has sought to give an evasive reply. The Committee
recommends that a concrete and specific action plan be prepared for removing the gaps.
(Para 5.22 & 5.23)
VI. NATIONAL VECTOR BORNE DISEASES CONTROL PROGRAMME (NVBDCP)
The Committee notes that a considerable period of time has elapsed since the
recommendation of the Group of Ministers was sent for approval. The Committee,
therefore, feels that the Ministry needs to be more proactive to push its case for approval
as delays in approvals lead to delay in implementation. (Para 6.9 & 6.10)
VII. NA TIONAL T.B. CONTROL PROGRAMME
The Committee notes that the default rate under the programme has declined from
6.9% in 2006 to 5.5% in 2011. The Committee expresses displeasure with the mere decline
of only 1.4% in the 5 year period mentioned above. The Committee feels that T.B being
a highly contagious disease, reduction of just 1.4% over a period of 5 years is not sufficient.
The Committee feels that the Department ought to take more stringent steps to increase
the tempo of curative as well as preventive aspects under the programme; otherwise all
measures taken so far would fall by wayside. (Para 7.4)
IX. NATIONAL TRACHOMA AND BLINDNESS CONTROL PROGRAMME
While making the above recommendation, the Committee had expected to be
provided with the details of progress made towards setting up of the Eye banks. However,
the Committee is dismayed to note that the Department has merely stated that funds have
been released to States/Union Territories for setting up of 57 Eye Banks. The Department
should have made efforts to collect the updated status of physical performance of the
project and apprised the Committee accordingly. The Committee, therefore, deprecates the
Department for its casual approach and exhorts it to use greater care while formulating its
reply in future. (Para 9.4)

ANNEXURE-VII TO PARA 16.7
BRIEF NOTE ON JAN AUSHADHI SCHEME
(QUALITY MEDICINES AT AFFORDABLE PRICES)
The Need - Over the years, India has developed a strong capability in producing generic medicines in
almost all the therapeutic categories. These medicines are being sold mostly as branded medicines,
which pushes up the retail price of these medicines. There is still a large population of poor people
in the country which finds it difficult to afford these medicines. In fact access to quality health care
is a challenge in a developing country like India. According to NSO estimates, upto 79% cost of health
care in rural areas is due to cost of medicines. This problem gets further aggravated as upto 80% of
expenditure on health care is out-of-pocket. With 65% of India’s population not having access to
modern health care (WHO estimates 2000 the entire problem is compounded several times.
Unbranded Generic Medicines Vs. Branded Medicines - Therefore, access to quality medicines at
affordable prices is a key challenge for the Government. In this connection the prices of branded
medicines are generally higher than generic medicines due to various reasons inter-alia including
branded drugs having patent protection and a number of drugs having limited regulation through the
Drug Prices Control Order, 1995 etc. A sample comparison of some of the prices is given below:
Name of salt Dosage Pack Market Generics Difference
Price (Rs.) Price (Rs.)
Antibiotic: Ciprofloxacin 250 mg 10 55.00 1 1.10 5 times higher
Pain Killer: Diclofenac 100 mg 10 36.70 3.50 10 times higher
Common Cold: Cetrizine 10 mg 10 20.00 2.75 7 times higher
Fever: Paracetamol 500 mg 10 10.00 2.45 4 times higher
Pain and Fever: Nimesulide 100 mg 10 25.00 2.70 9 times higher
Cough Syrup 110 ml bottle 33.00 13.30 2.5 times higher
For the above reasons therefore, making available medicines at affordable prices has been taken up by
the newly created Department of Pharmaceuticals.
Jan Aushadhi Campaign -  For fulfillment of this goal, a Campaign in the name of Jan Aushadhi
Campaign has been launched in 2008. The aim of this campaign is to make available quality medicines
at afforadable prices for all, especially the poor and the disadvantaged. Under this campaign, less priced
quality unbranded generic medicines will be made available through Jan Aushadhi Stores which
inherently are less priced but are of same and equivalent quality, efficacy and safety as compared to
branded generic medicines.
The generic medicines are being supplied in the first instance by the Central Pharma PSUs which will
ensure both quality and timely supply. Medicines not available currently with the CPSUs will be sourced
from quality SME units. This will also give support to the Pharma SME sector also as well as promote
public-private partnership and avenues for achievement of corporate social responsibilities geared
towards affordable medicare for the masses. The Jan Aushadhi Campaign has now been formalized as
Generic Drug Scheme with the approval of the Planning Commission.

124
Scheme Details -  Under this Scheme, the State Government has to provide space in Government
Hospital premises for the running of the outlets (JAS) Government hospitals, NGOs, Charitable
Organisations and public societies like Red Cross Society. Rogi Kalyan Samiti typically constituted for
the purpose can be operating agencies for the JAS. The operating agency for JAS is nominated on the
basis of the recommendations of the State Government. Operational expenditure is met from trade
margins admissible for the medicines. The State Government has to ensure prescription of unbranded
generic medicines by the Government doctors. The Jan Aushadhi Programme is accordingly being a
self sustaining business model not dependeation Government subsidies or assistance. It runs on the
principle of “Not for Profits but with Minimal Profits”. In order to incentivise and provide the initial
trigger for above, it is envisaged that the Central Government would provide, if need be, a token
amount of Rs. 50,000/- as infrastructural support and one-time financial support of Rs.2.00 lakhs to
NGO etc. on reimbursement basis, setting up the Jan Aushadhi Outlet.
Jan Aushadhi Stores -  The Jan Aushadhi Campaign of the Central Governemnt is exprected to make
a contribution by way of achieving the socio-economic goal of affordable health are through ensuring
availability of quality drugs at affordable prices for all. At present, 231 medicines are being supplied
in the 121 JAS opened (till 10
th May, 2012) in the States of Punjab, Haryana, Uttarakhand, Odisha,
Rajasthan, Andhra Pradesh, West Bengal, Himachal Pradesh, Jammu and Kashmir, Union Territories of
Chandigarh and Delhi. A list of Jan Aushadhi Opened is given below:
The scheme is also expected to lead to reduction of state health expenditure on branded medicines,
more patient coverage, popularization of the use of unbranded generic medicines which will bring down
the actual out-of-pocket costs of medicines, for the common man due to wider availability (at present
only 2% of the total medicines supplied in the market are unbranded medicines) and finally better and
more affordable health care driven by the reduction in costs of medicines as the majority coponent of
health care expenses.
People’s Participation -  The assistance sought is for just one time facilitative incentive to the Jan
Aushadhi outlet operating agency which would be an NGO/Charitable body/Cooperative body/health care
driven societies like the Red Cross Society/Rogi Kalyan Samiti, etc. who would do the actual operation
of the outlet on the principle of minimal profits obtained from the minimal margins included in the cost
of the medicine itself. There is no subsidy or recurring assistance envisaged either by the State or the
Central Gvoernment. Additionally it may be appreciated that if there are no dedicated outlets at strategic
locations, it may not be possible to promote the usage of unbranded generic medicines as mere media
campaigns without commensurate ready availability would be a wasted effort Cooperation of the State
Governments is essential for locating the outlets in the district hospital premises. The Generic Drugs
Scheme is an attempt in this direction based on a viable business model not requiring Government
subsidy. The Programme does not envisage grant of any upfront subsidy other than the assistance
indicated above to provide some support from the Government/BPPI to NGOs etc.
Benefits of the Scheme -  The Jan Aushadhi Campaign will help:
(i) Improve access to healthcare in as much as cost of treatment would come down
substatially. This would enable the public Health System to increase the coverage.
(ii) Secure a socio-economically viable mechanism/institutional arrangement for efficacions
sales of Pharma CPSU products, thereby improving their viability.
(iii) Promote and encourage private industry to sell their quality unbranded generic products
through these retail outlets.
(iv) Ensure successful implementation of the Jan Aushadhi campaign would dispel the myth
that quality of medicines is linked to price and demonstrate that quality medicines can be
sold at substantially lower prices.

125
(v) Educate dotors that unbranded generic medicines provide a better option than branded
products since quality of generic medicines can be equally efficacious and safe at much
lower prices.
(vi) Create Consumer awareness and involve private and charitable bodies and NGOs by
making them part of the campaign.
(vii) Reduce promotional cost and profits for the benefit of patients etc.
Constraints -
(i) Availability of space for Jan Aushadhi Stores at Hospital premises.
(ii) Prescription of medicines in generic form by Government Doctors/Private Doctors
(iii) A wareness among general public. Ministry of Health and Family Welfare may take suitable
action to help overcome the above constraints.

PREFACE
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Health and
Family Welfare, having been authorized by the Committee hereby present this 65 th Report of the
Committee on the proposal to introduce the Bachelor of Science (Community Health) course in the
country.
2. The Committee, at its meeting held on 18 th January, 2011, took note of the media reports
regarding Government’s move to introduce Bachelor of Rural Health Care (BRHC) course (now
Bachelor of Science (Community Health)) to overcome the shortage of the doctors in the country.
The Committee felt that it would be in the fitness of things to take up the subject for detailed
examination for studying all the pros and cons of the proposed move of the Government, since
the Committee felt that shortage of doctors looming in the country is a cause of serious concern
and needed to be addressed immediately.
3. The Committee deliberated on the issue in its meetings held on the 27
th January,
06th May, 1 st July, 22 nd, 27 th December, 2011, 20 th March, 09 th April, 8 th November, 2012,
8th February, 2013 and 13 th March, 2013.
4. During the course of examination of the subject mentioned above, the Committee heard the
views of Secretary, Department of Health and Family Welfare along with the Chairman, Board of
Governors and Medical Council of India on 27
th January, 22 nd December and 27 th December, 2011
and 8 th November, 2012. The Committee also had the benefit to hear the views of certain experts
in this field during its meetings held on 06 th May and 01 st July, 2011 (List of Experts at
Annexure-I). The Committee expresses its wholehearted thanks to all the witnesses who
enlightened the Committee with their views.
5. During the course of the examination of the subject under reference and finalization of its
Report thereon, the Committee relied upon the following documents/papers:–
(i) Status Note and Concept Note received Department of Health and Family Welfare
and Medical Council of India (MCI);
(ii) Report of the Task Force on Medical Education for the National Rural Health Mission
headed by Shri Javid Chowdhury, Ex-Secretary, Ministry of Health and Family
Welfare
(iii) O ral evidence tendered by the Secretary and other officers of the Department of
Health and Family Welfare and representatives of Board of Governors, Medical
Council of India;
(iv) Write-up received from Prof. K. Srinath Reddy, President, Public Health Foundation
of India and Dr. Meenakshi Gautham, Post doctorate fellow with the Institute of
Health Policy and Management, Erasmus University, Netherlands.
6. The Committee at its meeting held on the 13
th March, 2013 considered and adopted the
Draft Report.

7. For facility of reference and convenience, observations and recommendations of the
Committee have been printed in bold letters in the body of the Report.
 BRAJESH PATHAK
NEW D ELHI; Chairman,

Phalguna,  1934 ( Saka) Committee on Health and Family Welfare
