CHAPTER-I
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH REPLIES
OF THE GOVERNMENT HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE COMMITTEE
II. Budgetary Allocation
Recommendation/Observation
1.1 The Committee observes that the five new schemes/projects of the Department of Health
Research could not be made operational even during 2012-13 due to lack of approvals, though the
Department had come into existence in 2007 and become functional in 2008 with the appointment
of its first Secretary. The Committee is unable to comprehend the reasons for not getting the
required approvals even after a lapse of five years since the creation of the Department, which has
resulted in massive financial under-performance vis-à-vis the approved outlay of Rs. 4496.08 crore
for the Eleventh Plan. The Committee has been exhorting the Department to pay focused attention
for completing all pre-project formalities and obtaining necessary approvals on time so that the
budgeted funds are not locked up for want of approvals and surrendered later. The Committee is,
however, constrained to note that little attention seems to have been paid to its advice in this regard
which has resulted in persistent and substantial under-utilisation of budgeted funds. The first year
of the Twelfth Plan Period has already lapsed and the current year is the 2
nd year of the Twelfth
Plan. The Committee notes that the EFC approval for the three new Schemes were accorded, albeit
belatedly, on 22.03.2013. Two of the five new schemes have not been approved as yet. The
Committee, therefore, recommends to the Department to make more rigorous efforts and
proactively pursue approval of the remaining two schemes with the agencies concerned. The
Committee desires to be apprised of the updated status in this regard. The Committee also
recommends that a roadmap be chalked out to implement the Schemes and progress of their
implementation be monitored at highest level in the Department so that the desired outcomes are
achieved. The Committee desires that all the approved schemes should be made operational at least
during current financial year. Approvals to the remaining schemes may be accorded at the earliest
so that they may also become operational during the current year.
(Para 2.6)
Action Taken
1.2 Out of the five schemes formulated by the DHR, three schemes have already been
approved, viz. (1) Establishment of Model Rural Health Research Units (MRHRUs) in the States on
22.3.2013; (2) Establishment of Multi-disciplinary Research Units (MRUs) in Government Medical
Colleges on 27.6.2013 and (3) Establishment of a Network of Laboratories for Managing Epidemics
and Natural Calamities on 27.6.2013.
1.3 As regards the remaining two schemes, the appraisal process has been completed in
respect of the scheme regarding “Grants in Aid scheme for inter- sectoral Convergence and
Promotion and Guidance on Health Research” and the EFC meeting has been fixed on
27
th August, 2013. Regarding the scheme on “Human Resource Development for Health Research”
final appraisal note has been issued by the Planning Commission on 13.8.2013 and is being
processed for further action.
2

3
1.4 The matter is being vigorously pursued with the concerned departments and the position in
this regard is being reviewed periodically at the level of Secretary (DHR).
1.5 The Department has initiated the pre-implementation activities for all the five schemes by
inviting proposals. The Department has received requests from 64 Medical College for MRUs,
8 proposals for MRHRU and 10 proposals for virology laboratories from the various State
Governments. The DHR has received 531 concept proposals for GIA scheme and identified 30
faculty members for HRD fellowship for training within India and abroad.
1.6 Letters have been addressed to the Chief Secretaries and Principal Secretaries of Health/
Medical Education of the concerned States for completion of requisite formalities for
implementation of the shortlisted proposals in respect of the three approved schemes.
1.7 The Department plans to implement all the five schemes in the current financial year and
expect to utilize the allotted budget in full.
III. Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR)
Recommendation/Observation
1.8 The Committee places on record its appreciation for the achievements of ICMR during the
Eleventh Plan. However, in view of the dynamic international health research scenario and the
current and future health challenges of the country, the ICMR has an uphill task to accomplish and
milestones to achieve. The Committee would, therefore, like the ICMR to collaborate with
internationally acclaimed institutions in the field of Health research in order to facilitate a vibrant
and relevant health research system in the country.
(Para 3.3)
Action Taken
1.9 The Department is thankful to the committee for appreciation of XI Plan achievements. As
per committee reference to international collaboration, it is to be stated that ICMR collaborates with
many international agencies like WHO, NIH, CDC, etc and has a separate International Health
Division, which looks after this work and many MOUs, bilateral, tripartite agreements with many
countries have been signed in the field of health research, that help in building and enhancing health
research environment in the country.
1.10 ICMR is involved in collaborative programmes in biomedical research between India and
other countries as well as with national & international agencies such as Ministry of Science &
Technology, Indian and foreign missions and WHO, etc. There are few specific agreements signed
by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare with other countries and rest are those signed directly
by ICMR with international organizations/ institutions such as INSERM in France, German Federal
Ministry of Education and Research (BMBF) and Helmholtz Association (HGF) in Germany,
National Institutes of Health(NIH)/Centres for Disease Control (CDC) in USA, Canadian Institutes
of Health Research (CIHR) in Canada, University of Sydney and George Institute for International
Health in Australia, Medical Research Council (MRC) UK, London School of Hygiene and Tropical
Medicine (LSHTM) in UK, Karolinska Institute (KI)  in Sweden, Academy of Finland (AF).
1.11 The International Cooperation has helped the Indian scientists to establish collaborative links
with various countries for updating scientific knowledge, developing technologies and tools for
control and prevention of various diseases. It has facilitated resource generations, joint publications
and patents. It has increased research capacity building through trainings and fellowships and
helped in infrastructure development.

4
Recommendation/Observation
1.12 The Committee notes that a number of outcomes have been projected for the year 2013-14.
The Committee recommends that the desired outcomes be achieved within the targeted time-frame.
The Committee desires to be kept apprised of the achievements made vis-à-vis the targets set. The
Committee observes that it takes time to translate the research leads into tangible health products
or in application of the knowledge generated through research and a lot of work remains to be
done to bridge the gap between ‘what is known’ and ‘what is done’. Concerted efforts are required
to be made to bring research outcomes into application in the better interest of the public. The
Committee would, therefore, like to be apprised of the finding of the Committee constituted to
identify the leads from the completed extramural research projects. The Committee would also like
to be intimated of the specific health products/processes accruing from the above research projects.
(Para 3.10)
Action Taken
1.13 Leads emerging from intramural research as well as extramural projects during Eleventh
Plan are given in Annexure III. It is also to be added that a harvest group is proposed to be set-
up at the ICMR to identify the emerging leads from extramural projects and convert them into
products for public health. It is to further added that 30 new technologies (Annexure IV) ready
for transfer have been identified for the year 2013-14 and proposals have been invited from private
partners to take up these technologies to convert them into products for public use.
1.14 A fully functional Translational Research cell is already functioning in the ICMR for
translating the research leads under various subject heads into public health products. In addition,
area specific Committees have been/are being set up to be informed about the leads obtained from
completed extramural research projects.
Recommendation/Observation
1.15 The Committee observes that no single system of health care has the capacity to solve all
of the country’s health care needs. It is in this context that promotion of research in the area of
traditional medicines including Ayurveda, Naturopathy, Tibbia, Sowa-Rigpa and Homoeopathy
becomes vital for the public health care system. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the
research projects on traditional medicines be pursued vigorously and the innovations accruing
therefrom be introduced into public health service within a designated time-frame. The Committee
desires to be kept apprised of the success achieved in this regard.
(Para 3.17)
Action Taken
1.16 Though research on Herbal products is the domain of AYUSH Department under MoHFW
but ICMR also pursue and support research in Traditional Medicine for different disease conditions
and has a full fledged Institute viz., Regional Medical Research Centre, Belgaum, which is specially
working in this area. Major recent achievements of the Institute are: (a) scientific validation of
Herbal Medicine, (b) role of herbal medicine in treating diseases in the region; (c) preparation of
database of ethno medicinal plants of Western Ghats; (d) strengthening human resource in the area
of herbal and traditional medicine; (e) collaboration with traditional and herbal medicine practitioners
in the region to create awareness, promote scientific temperament, collect, collate and disseminate
relevant scientific information in the area of herbal medicine.
1.17 The centre has also been successful in: (a) preparation of database, establishment of
museum and herbal garden of ethno medicinal plants of Western Ghats and creating awareness

5
among visitors regarding traditional medicine system in the region; (b) providing services to
neighboring research institutes and NGOs in respect of identification and authentication of medicinal
plants and information on collection, cultivation and utility of medicinal plants; (c) establishment of
molecular and microbiology laboratory for testing of herbals against highly resistant bacteria. The
observations of the Committee are being informed to the Department of AYUSH.
1.18 Extramural research in traditional medicine is supported through Center for Advanced
Research, ad hoc research schemes and fellowships as well as through interagency programs:
(a) Centre for Advanced Research in Yoga and Neurophysiology at Swami
Vivekananda Yoga Research Foundation, Bangalore: Studies demonstrated the
overall neurophysiological correlates of meditation offer objective support for
meditation as therapy and as an effective strategy to perform better in cognitive tasks
and to organize higher brain functions specific to education in children and adults. The
centre has produced 7 Ph. D thesis and 8 MSc dissertations and four Annual month
long training programs and 7[1 international] short term research trainings were
conducted.
(b) Advanced Centre of Reverse Pharmacology in Traditional Medicine , Kasturba
Health Society, Mumbai: Studies demonstrated  that Curcuma longa  and curcumin
have proliferative effects in the hippocampal neural progenitors in aged rats, with
cognitive improvement. Nyctanthes abor-tristis showed antimalarial efficacy and safety
in vitro  and in vivo . W. somnifera  showed good tolerability and strength-enhancement
in human volunteers.
1.19 Presently 44 ad-hoc research projects, 40 fellowship projects are ongoing in traditional
medicine.
1.20 Novel methods have been established for in vitro  propagation of Ancistrocladus heyneanus
which is reported to have  anticancer activity. Random amplified polymorphic DNA (RAPD)
fingerprinting has been done of the medicinal plant Saraca asoca (Roxb.) used for treatment of
gynaecological disorders. A study on status of Methicillin Resistant Staphylococcus aureus  (MRSA)
infections was conducted which indicated the high prevalence of Methicillin resistant
Staphylococcus  aureus  (MSSA) with Panton Valentine Leukocidin (PVL) gene and further
epidemiological studies will be done in hospitals and community levels in the region. Molecular
studies were carried out on diphtheria and diarrheal pathogens and the studies helped in control of
outbreak in the region.
1.21 The work on non-codified plants used in traditional medicine practice is ongoing and two
projects completed as a result of which established exclusive herbarium and plant repository for
non codified plants and a laboratory was set up for screening of pathogenic microbial strain against
herbal extracts and building of analytical capacity to elucidate the compounds from such plants.
These non codified plants that are claimed to have therapeutic value by the grass root healers are
proposed to be studied for safety and efficacy studies. Around 800 traditional practices will be
taken for scientific validation under this programme.
ICMR-NIF joint collaborative programme in traditional practices: ICMR entered into a MoU
with National Innovation Foundation (NIF) for a period of five years on 23
rd June 2006. A task
force discussed the plan and formulated the structure of the proposal to be submitted to ICMR
so that scientific validation and value addition in traditional knowledge can help solve many day-
to-day problems of people. Under the scheme, value will be added by ICMR Labs and other
scientific institutions recognized by it to outstanding traditional herbal knowledge and innovations
to generate useful leads and share the benefits. The promising leads among the non-codified herbal
practices will be developed as marketable products. The MoU was further extended for a period

6
of next five years by DG, ICMR and is operative till 23 rd June 2016. Under ICMR- NIF
collaboration evaluation of anti typhoid and anti-diarrheal activities of medicinal plants claimed by
traditional healers have been undertaken. It is proposed to evaluate about 800 practices during 12 th
plan.
Collaboration with Department of AYUSH:  This collaboration aims at scientific validation of
traditional and other herbal formulations for HIV/AIDS cases. Under this collaboration following
facilities have been set up:
● Standardisation and Quality Control of traditional formulations at NIPER, Mohali and
SASTRA, Thanjavur
● In-vitro screening of the formulations for their anti HIV activity at NARI, Pune.
● Preclinical Pharmacology and Safety testing of the formulations at NIN, Hyderabad
● Monitoring of the clinical trials at Central Bio-statistical Monitoring Unit at NIE,
Chennai
1.22 Besides, ICMR has also brought out Monographs and Books on the medicinal values of
Herbal plants. During XI Plan, a total of 15 publications were brought out in the area of medicinal
plants viz, Quality Standards of Indian Medicinal Plants, Reviews on Indian Medicinal Plants,
Phytochemical Reference Standards of Selected Indian Medicinal Plants.
1.23 These publications are useful for developing plant drugs of adequate quality, safety and
efficacy of wider acceptance. Translate practically generated knowledge into direct utility for Indian
Drug Industry engaged in production of plant based drugs and for the Pharmacopoeial
Commissions in India & abroad for developing official quality standards on plant based drugs.
1.24 Review Monographs on Indian Medicinal plants  serve as comprehensive, informative and reliable
source of information providing information on new leads, thus helping in systematic and planned
evaluation of Medicinal plants, including drug design, basic and applied research. To develop
phytochemical Reference standard markers from select medicinal plants for standardization of drugs for
the stakeholders engaged in establishing and maintaining quality of medicinal plants and their products.
IV. Programmes for the North East
Recommendation/Observation
1.25 The Committee welcomes the initiatives taken by the Department to undertake studies and
projects specific to North Eastern Region and exhorts that focused attention be paid to the
implementation of the above projects by way of streamlined monitoring so that tangible outcomes
could be achieved and benefits emerging there from percolate down to the people.
(Para 4.3)
Action Taken
1.26 ICMR supports research activities in NE Region and 10% of the budget is spent on
research studies in NE area. During XI Plan period total 63 Projects were funded by the ICMR
in North Eastern areas.
1.27 A Centre for Advanced Research in the area of Medicinal plants has been set up in Kolkata
and Manipur. The Centre has developed DNA Fingerprinting pattern to establish species specific
DNA markers that may be used for identification of Species specificity of some medicinal plants
like Zanthoxylum acanthopodium, Zanthoxylum oxyphyllum,  Acorus calamus  Curcuma longa,

7
Curcuma caesia and curcuma zedoaria  which are used for Alzheimer’s disease, anticancer, anti-
inflammatory activity. The experimental material, viz. wild landraces, for the species under study
were collected by Botanical Survey of India from widely different locations at different altitudes
in North Eastern and Eastern India under this project.  Training has been imparted on Plant DNA
Fingerprinting and chemical analysis of medicinal potential to young faculty members and students.
The work has resulted into 6 publications.
1.28 Further the fingerprinting pattern to establish species specific DNA markers set up by this
centre can be widely used by the pharmaceutical companies to ensure the authenticated use of the
various plant materials for preparation of the drugs so as to ensure its efficacy. The centre is being
approached by such companies to obtain training of their scientists on the same.
1.29 The North East India also shares international borders with neighbouring countries like
Nepal, China, Myanmar and Bangladesh, and being a gateway to South East Asia, attains a specific
importance to various problems due to communicable diseases and cross border transmission.
Among them are: vector borne diseases; viral diseases including dengue/DHF, JE, chikungunia,
AES, West Nile virus, measles hepatitis, HPV, HIV/STDs; rickettesial diseases; acute diaarhoeal
diseases; bacterial diseases including TB and some parasitic diseases (including neurocysticercosis
(because of close association with pigs), paragonimiasis etc.). The region also has biodiversity rich
herbs, plants, micro flora and fauna, which must be explored for health benefits and their use as
natural products in treatment for various micro organisms and diseases. In this backdrop, priority
areas of research in communicable diseases that can be pursued in the North East Region, have
been identified, with an objective to put up these areas on the website of ICMR and invite ‘call
for proposals’. The projects that will be received subsequently will be short-listed and reviewed in
a Committee of Experts before placing the same in the NE-PRC for funding by ICMR. The focus
of NE projects is primarily to conduct translational research and to cater the problems of North
East for the benefit of people and patient welfare.
1.30 Under a special North East Initiative, several schemes have been initiated which include
providing support for full proposals through the North East Project Review Committee, providing
seed money grant up to Rs.10 lakhs to the new researchers of the NE Region. Some research units
are also being set up in all the medical colleges of NE Region. All these schemes are designed to

II. Budgetary Allocation
Recommendation/Observation
2.1 The Committee notes that there is significant variation between the Budget Estimates and
the actual expenditure incurred in respect of the five new schemes of the Department. Persistent
mismatch between the Budget Estimates and the actual expenditure indicates that budget
formulation is being done without applying proper financial yardsticks. The Committee feels that
there is an imperative need to minimize the huge mismatch between the Budget Estimates and the
actual expenditure so as to observe the fiscal norms in letter and spirit. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that corrective measures be initiated and implemented for realistic projection of fund
requirements of the Department in future.
(Para 2.7)
Action Taken
2.2 The provisions of General Financial Rules and the guidelines issued by the Ministry of
Finance (Budget Division) for budget formulation, financial management and periodical
monitoring are duly followed by the Department of Health Research. Since all the schemes
formulated by DHR are new schemes to fulfil the objectives as per the mandate of the newly
created department, budget provisions for these schemes are being made from time to time
based on the total estimated project cost as well as the year-wise phasing of physical and
financial targets of the schemes. It is necessary to make requisite budgetary provisions for the
schemes as in the absence of this, the schemes are not taken up for consideration and
appraisal. However, despite best efforts by the Department, the schemes could not be approved
during the Eleventh Plan.
2.3 Now since the three schemes have already been approved and sanctioned and the
remaining two schemes are also expected to be cleared during the current financial year,
maximum utilization of budgeted funds is expected with the implementation of the schemes. The
suggestion of the Committee for making realistic projection of fund requirements is noted for
compliance.
Recommendation/Observation

Health Research and is responsible for formulation, coordination and promotion of bio-medical
research in the country. The Committee, therefore, notes with serious concern the likely adverse
impact of the funds crunch on the intramural and extramural research priorities of ICMR. The
Committee desires that Planning Commission/Ministry of Finance may reconsider the allocation for
ICMR for the Twelfth Plan after making a fair assessment.

II. BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
Recommendation/Observation
3.1 The Committee observes that scientific knowledge generated through health and bio-medical
research is used to develop drugs, diagnostics, vaccines and devices that ultimately find place in
the health care systems of the country. It is also worth mentioning that health research has a vital
role to play in the discovery and development of indigenous health products. Taking all these
factors into account, the Committee apprehends that allowing the new schemes to be plagued with
under-funding from the very beginning would prove detrimental to generation of new knowledge
in the area of health research. The Committee, therefore, lends its support for enhancement of
funds for the schemes at the RE stage. The Committee, simultaneously, recommends to the
Department to pay focused attention to more efficient deployment of the available resources.
(Para 2.10)

available resources.

was piloted in the year 2010 through the ICMR system as adhoc project. The entire initiative was
taken up in a project mode for a period of five years. As of now, fifteen laboratories in fourteen
States of the country are functional.

II. BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
Recommendation/Observation
1.1 From a glance of the above Table, the Committee notes that the funds allocated over the
period of Eleventh Plan and Annual Plan 2012-13 has increased steadily. However, the Committee
is constrained to observe that in a time of increasing demand due to demographic pressures, public
expectations and medical advances there was substantial and persistent under-utilization of the
budgeted funds during the Eleventh Plan and Annual Plan of 2012-13. The Committee desires that
the processes of allocation and utilization of funds should be mutually reinforcing instead of being
parallel. That the savings occurred under the Plan head underlines the fact that the development
activities might have been adversely affected in the health sector. The Committee, accordingly
impresses upon the Department that in future utilization must reflect the allocation policy objectives
to the extent possible. (Para 2.2)
Action Taken
1.2 Noted for compliance.
Recommendation/Observation
1.3 The Committee’s examination of the following major heads of account as per the
background material furnished by the Department has revealed recurrent and persistent sub-optimal
utilization of budgetary provisions (Plan) during the last three Financial years (Annexure-A).
Actual expenditure incurred in respect of some of the major Institutions/projects/initiatives
of Department for the last three financial years is as under Annexure-B. (Para 2.7)
Action Taken
1.4 Matter of Record.
Recommendation/Observation
1.5 From a perusal of the above Tables, the Committee observes that with such level of
underutilization of funds, the financial objectives and target achievement of the Department would
suffer to a large extent. The Department has informed that during the Eleventh Plan the extent of
savings on the Capital Account has been Rs.2883.25 crore. Most of the savings were due to slow
progress of capital work and slow pace of procurement of equipments. The Committee observes
with deep concern that savings under the Capital section implies that it will impede the
2

3
developmental activities. Slow progress in capital work would critically hamper both the quality of
care provided and the ability of the system as a whole to respond to increased demand in this
sector. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should take concrete steps to
address this issue by means of prudent assessment of the fund requirement and design effective
mechanism to make a balance between spending and savings. (Para 2.8)
Action Taken
1.6 The observations of the Committee have been noted for compliance.
Recommendation/Observation
1.7 The Committee desires to be apprised of the hurdles faced by the Department in the path
of utilization of allocated funds and delivering the objectives and the steps initiated and pursued by
the Department to streamline formulation of the budgetary requirements in a realistic fashion and
also to expedite necessary approvals for operationalization of various formulated schemes/projects.
(Para 2.9)
Action Taken
1.8 Major hurdle in the path of utilisation of funds during 2012-13 was economy instructions
of Ministry of Finance dated 14
th November, 2012 which necessitated submission of all UCs under
all the Schemes of Government of India. To overcome this hurdle, the Ministry has taken action
and has appointed Nodal Officers to the various States for settlement of pending UCs so that
allocated funds are optimally utilised during the current year.
Recommendation/Observation
1.9 Taking all the above factors into consideration, the Committee recommends that the
Department should once again assess its fund requirements realistically and thereafter move the
Planning Commission for augmentation of financial resources for health sector for 2013-14 at RE
stage. The Committee would like to be apprised of the follow-up action taken in this regard.
(Para 2.10)
Action Taken
1.10 The observations of the Committee have been noted for compliance. The appropriate action
in this regard is being taken and all the Programme Divisions are being requested to re-assess their
requirement so that the revised proposals can be submitted to Ministry of Finance for consideration
at RE stage.
Recommendation/Observation
1.11 The Committee is deeply concerned that a large number of UCs are still pending under both
the Centrally Sponsored and Central Sector Schemes. The additional measure taken by the
Department by organizing reconciliation week has also not resulted in optimizing the liquidation of
UCs. The Committee desires to be informed of the reasons given by the States for non-submission
of UCs. The Ministry should also verify the physical progress matching the utilization. The
Committee, accordingly, recommends that the Department needs to have a prudent assessment of
the reasons for pendency of such a large number of Utilization Certificates and reframe action plans
for liquidation thereof. (Para 2.13)

4
Action Taken
1.12 The reframed action plan for the clearance of large number of pending UCs is as under:
1. The Ministry of Health and FW has appointed Additional Secretaries/Joint Secretaries/
Directors as nodal officers from divisions of this Ministry, releasing grant to the
States, to visit the concerned States to settle the pendency of related UCs and submit
their reports to the competent authority.
2. A calendar is being prepared by the sanction issuing authority to call the State
Government officials to reconcile their pending UCs and provide details of expenditure
and audited accounts.
Recommendation/Observation
1.13 The Committee in para 1.21 of its fifty-fourth Report had recommended for a speedy action
on the observations as contained in audit paras. Reiterating the recommendation, the Committee
would further suggest that audit paras should not be neglected. Timely action should be taken on
audit paras. (Para 2.15)
Action Taken
1.14 The position of pending ATNs is monitored regularly by holding Special Audit Committee
Meetings in the Ministry.
● The Audit Office has been requested to expedite vetting comments on ATNs already
sent to them.
● The matter is being followed up regularly with DGACE by deputing officer concerned
to that office.
III. CENTRAL GOVERNMENT HEALTH SCHEME
Recommendations/Observations
1.15 The Committee is disappointed to note the continuous trend of under-utilization of Plan
Funds during the Eleventh Plan and in the year 2012-13, more so when the Department has sought
enhanced funds at RE stage during the Eleventh Plan and 2012-13. The actual expenditure figures
also indicate that the Department could not even utilize the funds allocated at BE stage except
during 2009-10. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that the Department should devise
strategies to utilize the allocated funds optimally before proposing the revised estimate so that the
funds are not unnecessarily blocked and remain unspent. The Committee could not understand why
such higher allocation was sought during successive years inspite of under-utilisation in the earlier
years. The Department should look into the matter. (Para 3.3)
1.16 Despite continuous under-utilization of funds during the Eleventh Five Year Plan, there is
enhanced allocation in Plan funds to Rs. 89.92 crore in 2013-14 from Rs. 85.26 crore in RE
2012-13. The Committee has been informed that the enhanced funds allocation under Plan Head
will be utilized for meeting the expenditure on account of salary and wages, purchase of medicines
and all other administrative expenses to be incurred by some CGHS cities for which budgets are
allocated under Plan head only. Cities where CGHS Wellness Centres are being run under Plan Head
are: Chandigarh, Bhopal, Bhubaneswar, Guwahati, Shillong, Dehradun, Jabalpur, Ranchi and
Thiruvananthapuram. The Committee is of the view that for ensuring optimum utilization of funds
in CGHS the Department needs to undertake a lot of ground work. (Para 3.5)

5
Action Taken
1.17 The point made by the Hon’ble Committee has been noted. The Department shall make all
possible efforts to ensure maximum utilization of plan funds, especially the funds allocated for
Capital Works and funds earmarked for NE regions. The plan funds allocated for Capital Works
are generally placed at the disposal of CPWD which takes its own time for selection of contractor
and execution of work. The time involved in completing such mandatory process by CPWD as per
the laid down provisions of GFR results in under-utilization of plan funds. This issue has been
taken up in past with CPWD to expedite the process. The Department shall make further efforts
with CPWD to get the things expedited to ensure maximum utilization of funds. The Department
shall also take necessary steps to ensure maximum utilization of recurring funds allocated under
plan funds.
Recommendation/Observation
1.18 On a query regarding the current pendency of settlement of Medical Reimbursement Claims
(MRC) of CGHS beneficiaries, the Committee has been apprised that a total of 4061 claims
involving about Rs.16.36 crore were under process in CGHS all over the country, at the end of
December, 2012. It has also been informed that a maximum time limit of 45 days has been fixed
for settlement of Medical Reimbursement Claims (MRC) and that a report of the MRCs pending
beyond 45 days will be sent by the respective Additional Directors to the Directorate on a monthly
basis. The Committee welcomes the efforts made by the Department to bring about a significant
reduction in pendency of reimbursement claims and hopes that the Department would be able to
bring this pendency further down with its sincere efforts. The Committee likes the Department to
diligently monitor the effective implementation of the said procedure to protect the interests of the
beneficiaries. (Para 3.7)
Action Taken
1.19 Department is making continuous efforts to make reimbursement of medical claims of the
pensioners/CGHS beneficiaries hassle free and in the shortest possible time. Sometimes the
settlement of Medical Reimbursement Claims (MRC) takes a longer time for want of requisite
documents from the beneficiary and also opinion from specialists of Government hospitals.
However, Instructions have been issued to settle the Medical Reimbursement Claims within the
shortest possible time. A maximum time-limit of 45 days has been fixed for this purpose within
which the claim should be settled. The Department shall continue its endeavour to address the
MRC related issues on priority.
Recommendation/Observation
1.20 The Committee notes that the initiatives taken by the Department so far to combat the
serious problem of shortage of doctors and staff in CGHS Wellness Centres have not been enough.
The Committee strongly feels that to deal with the issue of perennial shortage of doctors, CMOs
and other supporting staff in CGHS Wellness Centres, initiatives should be taken to design a
framework for optimum utilization of the available resources to fill up the vacancies and then
sustain that level so as to deal with the problem in an efficient manner. (Para 3.10)
Action Taken
1.21 There is an overall shortage of medical and paramedical professionals in the country and
the Government is making efforts to address this problem. CGHS, like other Government

6
institutions is also facing the shortage of doctors. So far as fresh recruitments are concerned UPSC
makes recommendations every year for direct appointment of doctors and also for filling vacancies
of promotional posts. However, many of the selected candidates against direct recruitment do not
join CGHS. Retired doctors have been hired on contract basis against some of the vacant posts
to manage the operations depending on the immediate need. The existing CGHS Wellness Centres
and other formations are working in efficient manner with the human resources available at present.
However, the point made by the Hon’ble Committee is noted and the Department shall make further
efforts to fill up the vacancies and strengthen the human resources wherever required to improve
the functioning of CGHS.
Recommendations/Observations
1.22 The Committee was apprised that timings of CGHS dispensaries have been revised so as
to provide extended hours of the Wellness Centres. The Department has informed that to overcome
the problem of shortage of doctors and paramedical staff and ensure optimum utilization of scarce
manpower resources, it was decided to change the working hours of the CGHS dispensaries from
the current timings of 7.30 AM to 1.30 PM to 8.00 AM to 3.00 PM with 30 minutes of lunch
break. The new timings have been implemented in Delhi NCR with effect from 1st April, 2013.
However, six dispensaries (including the VIP dispensaries), which are operational for 24 hours, are
not covered under the revised timings. The Department has also informed that with the
computerization of all CGHS dispensaries and universal application and portability of CGHS cards,
one can easily avail the CGHS facilities from any dispensary/First Aid Post near to his residence
or place of work as per his/her convenience and there is no compulsion to go to his parent
dispensary for medical consultation and medicines. The proposed working hours will rather be
more convenient for the serving employees as it will provide longer effective working hours for
availing the facilities. (Para 3.11)
1.23 The Committee is dismayed by the contradictory information received from many
beneficiaries that their grievances were not heard in Wellness Centres other than the parent CGHS
dispensaries. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that the Department should ensure
that effective implementation of the new initiative taken; otherwise it would be a futile exercise on
papers. The Committee also feels that double shifts in CGHS Wellness Center would be more
beneficial for a large number of beneficiaries as well as the staff. The beneficiaries need not take
leave from their offices to visit the dispensary and larger number of patients can be covered in
a day and the burden will get distributed between the shifts so as to make it easier on the staff.
(Para 3.12)
Action Taken
1.24 The Department had introduced the complete portability of CGHS cards across the country
vide its OM dated 16-03-2011 enabling CGHS beneficiaries to avail medical consultation and
medicines from any CGHS wellness Centre. Instructions have also been issued vide Circulars dated
17-12-2012, 08-02-2013 and 22-05-2013 directing the CMO I/Cs and other officers concerned to
enforce it scrupulously without any discrimination. They are also being sensitized regularly through
periodic meetings by the senior officers to implement the orders in letter and spirit.
1.25 So far as introduction of double shifts in CGHS wellness centres is concerned, it is to
mention that double shifts were introduced in August 2011 in CGHS Wellness Centres at Noida,
Gurgaon and Faridabad and the response received was not encouraging. Keeping in view the
scarcity of the professionally qualified medical and paramedical human resources in CGHS,
introduction of double shifts may not be a feasible proposition.

7
Recommendations/Observations
1.26 On the query of the Committee on the steps being taken to ensure that the instructions
issued to the CMO in charge of all the Wellness Centres to stop the pilferage of medicines is being
scrupulously followed, the Department informed that CMOs in-Charge are expected to adhere to
the detailed instructions issued to them in this regard. To ensure that the instructions are followed
by them properly, the following steps have been taken:
(a) The CMOs In-charge are sensitized about it regularly by the Additional Director of the
concerned zone/ city in the monthly meetings.
(b) Surprise Inspections are carried out by the superior officers to verify the stock of
drugs/medicines in the dispensary stores /counters.
(c) Internal Audit Unit of Vigilance Division of CGHS does surprise visits to know as to
whether the guidelines to stop pilferage of medicines are being adhered to.
(d) Appropriate actions are taken in case of non-compliance of the instructions.
(e) To exercise an effective check on pilferage of medicines from the CGHS Wellness
centres, an ‘SMS Alert system’ has been introduced. A system generated message is
sent to the CGHS beneficiaries indicating that he/she has been issued medicines from
the CGHS dispensary. Registration of Mobile number has also been made compulsory.
(Para 3.13)
1.27 In this regard the Committee recommends that in addition to the steps already taken by the
Department, it should also be ensured that there is no leakage at the transit stage. Comparable
measures of quality should also be worked out at the earliest. (Para 3.14)
Action Taken
1.28 The following measures have been taken to ensure quality of medicines supplied to CGHS
and to prevent pilferage of CGHS medicines;
1. Whenever medicines are procured by MSD through sources other than HSCC or under
Pilot Project, in-house analysis report of the drugs is submitted by the Manufacturer/
Distributor. As far as procurement through HSCC is concerned, a joint team of HSCC
and CGHS draws random 2
nd samples from the supplied drugs under inspection and
sent to pre-designated authorized Laboratories and Govt. Laboratories for mandatory
testing.
2. Same procedure is followed for Pilot project drugs, except for the samples for
2
nd analysis are drawn by the CMO In-charges.
3. For Life Saving Drugs and supplies by authorized local chemists, quality control
measures are taken by state Drug Control Department.
In addition, the following steps are taken in the Medical stores Depot, CGHS to ensure
transparency and accountability;
● Proper maintenance of stock records.
● Stock position/availability of medicines can be viewed online by the CMO I/Cs for
proper utilisation of medicines.
● Short supplies/over supplies of medicines are looked into immediately for taking
remedial measures.

8
However, the suggestion made by Hon’ble Committee about checking pilferage of medicines
is noted and CGHS will ensure that no leakage takes place at any stage. CGHS is also committed
for ensuring supply of quality drugs and medicines to its beneficiaries.
Recommendation/Observation
1.29 The Committee would like to be apprised of the details on how the Department would utilize
the non-plan allocation for improving the quality of medicines being provided to the beneficiaries.
(Para 3.16)
Action Taken
1.30 In addition to the measures indicated in the previous para, the following measures have also
been taken to enforce quality assurance in the medicines supplied to CGHS beneficiaries;
1. Random Samples of pilot project drugs, sent to approved labs to ensure quality of
drugs.
2. Bar coding of all the supplies received has been introduced to stop pilferage and ensure
quality.
Recommendation/Observation
1.31 The Committee feels that still much is required to be done in this direction as the feedback
generally received by the Committee as regards the satisfaction level of beneficiaries is not positive.
A serious introspection as regards the sufficiency of efforts made, is required. Besides, the
Committee is of the opinion that effective communication strategies should be designed to
encourage positive partnership among the different levels of officials so as to generate
organizational support for reforms. The Committee desires that patient satisfaction level should
regularly be reviewed. (Para 3.18)
Action Taken
1.32 A new format of Inspection report for wellness centres is being devised with inputs from
the concerned authority.
Beneficiaries are participating indirectly in the management and operation of CGHS Wellness
Centres through their representatives in the Local Advisory Committees set up at the Wellness
Centre level under the chairmanship of the CMO In charges. In addition to the Help line, a ‘Help
Desk’ has recently been set up to provide answers to the queries of the beneficiaries. The FAQs
have also been made exhaustive and more informative to help beneficiaries availing CGHS facilities
in a better manner.
The Department shall continue its endeavour to make CGHS more user friendly and service
oriented.
Recommendation/Observation
1.33 Any policy for revising the rates should be based on long- term perspectives instead of
emphasizing on the cost containment with a short- term perspective. The Committee recommends
that the Department may revisit its policies on revising the rates and rationalize the new package
rates so that the CGHS beneficiaries are no longer deprived of highly specialized medical care and
diagnostic facilities. The rates should be so fixed to attract the best hospitals in the private sector.
(Para 3.20)

9

The requirement of Machinery and Equipment of each Centre/Department in AIIMS is

1.65 The C ommittee takes a serious view of the fake, substandard, spurious and adulterated
medicines being detected in such large number of cases. This amounts to playing with the lives of
the people. This can not be tolerated. All the States should be asked to prosecute all the cases. The
CDSCO may regularly review the progress and apprise the Committee. The Committee recommends

(SOPs) for approval of new drugs and clinical trials should be expedited. (Para 16.10)
Action Taken
1.66 A survey to assess the extent of spurious drugs in the country was conducted in the
year 2009 by the Central Drugs Standard Control Organization (CDSCO). The survey was
statistically designed by the Indian Statistical Institute, Hyderabad. Under the study, 24,136 samples
of 62 brands of drugs were drawn from different outlets spread over the country. The survey
revealed that the extent of drugs found spurious was 0.046% only. Further, as per the information
made available by the State Drugs Controllers in respect of the drugs samples tested during
last three years, the percentage of substandard drugs varied from 5.70% in 2008-09 to 4.54% in
2011-12.
1.67 Notwithstanding these figures, the Government has taken the following measures to check
Spurious/Sub-standard Drugs in the country:
1. The Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 was amended by the Drugs and Cosmetics
(Amendment) Act, 2008 to provide for more stringent penalties for manufacture and
trade of spurious and adulterated drugs. Certain offences have also been made
cognizable and non-bailable. 
2. The Drugs and Cosmetics (Amendment) Act, 2008 has also enabled setting up of
special designated courts for speedy disposal of cases to deal with the cases of
offences under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act. 16 States/UTs have already set up these
special Courts. 

19
3. Guidelines for taking action on samples of drugs declared spurious or not of standard
quality in the light of enhanced penalties under the Drugs and Cosmetics (Amendment)
Act, 2008 have been forwarded to the State Drugs Controllers for implementation. 
4. A Whistle Blower Scheme has been initiated by the Government to encourage vigilant
public participation in the detection of movement of spurious drugs in the country.
Under this scheme, the informers would be suitably rewarded for providing concrete
information in respect of movement of spurious drugs to the regulatory authorities. 
5. On the basis of an Order of the Hon’ble High Court of Allahabad in the Criminal
(Misc.) Writ Petition No. 16212/2008 – Brahmaji vs. State of UP and Others, the
Government had constituted a Task Force to examine the feasibility of networking and
tracking the drugs distribution system in the country from the manufacturer to the
retailer to secure the entire supply chain and detect spurious drugs available in the
market. Different options through the use of information technology were considered
by the Task Force, including providing bar code on the label of the drugs, for
identifying and tracking their movement from the manufacturer to the consumer. On
the basis of the recommendations of the Task Force and further consultation with the
stakeholders, the Government conducted a study with the help of the National
Informatics Centre to examine the feasibility of networking and tracking the drugs
distribution system in the country from the manufacturer to the retailer by the use of
modern information technological tools to detect spurious drugs available in the market.
6. Overseas inspections of drug manufacturing sites to ensure quality of imported bulk
drugs were started in 2011.
7. 216 additional posts were created in 2008 and 2009 for strengthening CDSCO
headquarters and ports/zonal offices. It has further, been proposed to create 1045

II. BUDGETARY PROVISIONS
Recommendation/Observation
1.1 The Committee feels that funds should not be a constraint with respect to vital Schemes
like NRHM-RCH Flexible Pool, NUHM-Flexible pool, National Programme for control of Blindness,
Health Care for Elderly, National Programme for Control of Deafness, National Tobacco Control
Programme, National Programme for Prevention and Control of Cancer, Diabetes, Cardiovascular
Diseases and Stroke. No allocation has been made for assistance to States for Capacity Building
(Burns) under the NHM. Similarly the funds allocated to the Family Welfare- Central sector is quite
less than the funds sought. The Committee, therefore recommends to the Department that in order
to convince the Ministry of Finance/Planning Commission, it needs to put in place a strong and
effective physically and financially prudent system which is able to absorb the funds allocated to
it, which does not seem to be the case now in view of the persistent underutilization of the funds
allocated to it year after year under NRHM. The Committee recommends that the Department’s
vision to undertake Universal Health Coverage should not suffer due to non-allocation of funds for
NUMH and dropping of implementation thereof. The Committee is very much concerned with the
sorry state of affairs of healthcare facilities presently available to urban poor particularly those
living in urban slums. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should make all
out efforts to get more funds at RE stage for implementation of some of the schemes under
NUHM. Besides, the funds meant for NRHM should not be directed for NUHM. (Para 2.8)
Action Taken

the Finance Minister, vide letter dated 13

Recommendation/Observation
1.3 The Committee feels that the total Expenditure by Government (Central and State
Governments combined) as a percentage of GDP has merely increased from 1.27 in 2007-08 to
1.29 in 2011-12 which is a very telling comment on the state of affairs of public spending on
Health which directly translates into high Out-of-Pocket expenses for a majority of population. The
Committee observes that given the fact that a significant percent of India’s population is
impoverished every year due to illness of a family member, there is an imperative need to increase
the total expenditure at the Centre and the States level to at least 3% of GDP. Since the States
are themselves under fiscal stress, it is for the Centre to assign a significant part of its resources
towards health care. The Committee hopes that the Department would be able to live up to the
contention of the Planning Commission for increasing the total Government expenditure, both at
centre and state level as a proportion of GDP in the Twelfth Plan from 1.94 percent in the last
year of the Eleventh Plan to 3.04 percent in the corresponding year of the twelfth Plan given the

1.12 Mandatory notification of all TB cases by Health Establishments in country, both public and
private sectors
● Guidance tool with mechanism for TB Notification was developed by Central TB
Division (also available on tbcindia website)
● Contact details of nodal officers for TB notification in each district in the country was
compiled (also available on tbcindia website)
● Sensitization of State and District TB Officers and Health staff was conducted across
the country to initiate TB notification.
● Wide publicity was given for TB notification by printing the copy of Government
Order in leading national and local newspapers throughout the country.
● Till date over 54000 Health Establishments (both public and private) have reported /
notified 12,33,170 TB cases.
1. Introduction of case based web based system of electronic recording and reporting of TB
cases (Nikshay)
● Central TB Division (CTD) in collaboration with National Informatics Centre (NIC)
developed Case based web based system of electronic recording and reporting of TB
cases (Nikshay) which was launched on 15th May, 2013 after quick testing of
feasibility. More than 3500 users have been created with login IDs at different levels
including Tuberculosis Unit (TU), District, States/UT and national level. 38000 health
facilities have been mapped from which details of TB cases are entered in the
software.
● User manuals were developed and master trainers trained at national level and software
was launched in May, 2012. Rapid training cascade was completed in training of
provincial level (50), district level (668) and block level (~8000) data entry operators
using training videos in English and Hindi, user manual and demonstrations. All health
officers and TB Officers were sensitized by August, 2012.
● The application is used for monitoring and tracking of individual patient notified to the
Revised National Tuberculosis Control Programme. Till now, we have 1.2 million cases
entered in this application. This ensures appropriate and effective treatment of all TB
cases to prevent drug resistant TB. This application also includes details of Multi-Drug
Resistant (MDR) patients and HIV associated Tuberculosis. Auto generation of
Programme reports and epidemiological analysis is also being done.
2. Early diagnosis of drug resistant TB cases by expansion of MDR-TB suspect criteria to
include all re-treatment smear positive TB cases and positives on any follow up.
● RNTCP has conducted appraisal of all districts implementing DOTS for rolling out
PMDT services and state has been provided the appraisal report with recommendation
for the district. All districts throughout the country started PMDT services by March
2013.
● Laboratory capacity in state and treatment capacity at DR-TB center has been
expanded across the country and more and more districts are expanding MDR-TB
suspect criteria to include all re-treatment smear positive TB cases.

54
● Currently 470 districts are following MDR-TB suspect criteria to include all re-
treatment smear positive TB cases and positives on any follow up to ensure early
diagnosis of drug resistant TB cases.
3. CB-NAAT for early and additional case detection.
● RNTCP is conducting the pilot feasibility study with objective of potential impact of
introducing CB-NAAT for the detection of TB and Rifampicin resistance at TU level to
generate evidence for RNTCP scale-up for CB-NAAT at 18 sites across 12 states.
● The impact will be measured by additional number of cases of TB and MDR-TB
detected compared to the sputum smear microscopy across the 18 sites across
12 states.
4. Early diagnosis of HIV in TB patients (in high prevalence areas).
● Provider Initiated HIV Testing and Counselling (PITC) among Presumptive TB cases
(TB suspects) is now a policy which is being implemented on priority in High HIV
prevalent states/settings. In low HIV prevalent states/settings – HIV testing among
presumptive TB cases should be routinely implemented in the age-group of 25-54 years
at places where there are co-located TB and HIV testing facilities.
● The state of Karnataka was implementing PITC among TB suspects in 2012 as a
feasibility study which was subsequently continued after the study. Out of the
31 districts, the proportion of of presumptive TB cases knowing their HIV status was
nearly 46% (range 10-3% and 9% range (9-29%) were found to be HIV positive.
● During the supervision and monitoring visits, it was observed that there was significant
proportion of TB suspects who know their HIV status or were referred from ICTC/
ART centres. The other high HIV prevalent states like Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu and
Maharashtra are in the process of implementation.
5. TB and diabetes patients for early diagnosis of both the diseases
● A state-wide representative sample of TB patients in Kerala was conducted. Wherein
out of 552 TB patients screened 243 (44%) patients were found to be having Diabetes
Mellitus.
● Subsequently a pilot project was undertaken for bi-directional screening within the
routine healthcare setting across the country at eight tertiary care hospitals and eight
tuberculosis units.
● The study has shown that out of 8109 TB patients who were tested for Diabetes
Mellitus 1084 (13%) were found to have Diabetes Mellitus. Whereas, 254 (1.9%) TB
patients were detected out of 13,961 diabetic patients screened for TB.
● Based on the result the programme has made a policy to screen all TB patients for
Diabetes in 100 districts where National Programme for Prevention and Control of
Cancer, Diabetes, Cardiovascular Diseases and Stroke (NPCDCS) is being implemented.

patients will also be extended to those districts.
Revision of dosing for paediatric TB cases with increasing the number of weight bands for

II. BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
Recommendation/Observation
3.1 Approved outlay for National Health Mission (NHM) for the Twelfth Plan is Rs.193405.71
crores as against the projected outlay of Rs.219702.45 crores. Further against a projected demand
for Rs.32,520.13 crore for NHM, the Planning Commission has approved an outlay of Rs.20999.00
crore for 2013-14. The Committee is aware that public spending on health was targeted to be
increased to 2.5% of GDP at the launch of NRHM in 2005. However, as per figures quoted by
the Economic Survey 2012-13, public expenditure on health is just 1.29% of GDP. Private
expenditure on health is 2.9% of GDP. The Committee observes that even if the level of
government expenditure on health is increased to 2.5% of GDP, there would still be a very
substantial health care expenditure which is out-of-pocket payments made by the households in
time of health distress. The cost of health care services in the private sector is so exorbitant that
it is just unaffordable for the poor and the under-privileged. It is in this context that the reduction
in approved outlay of Rs.193405.71 crore for NHM for the Twelfth Plan against the projected
demand of Rs.219702.45 crore is cause for extreme concern to the Committee. Keeping in view
the fact that illness of a family member is the most common reason leading to a financial crisis
among poor households, the Committee lends its full support for greater health outlays. The
Committee, simultaneously, recommends that the Department should strengthen its monitoring
mechanism so as to ensure that the available resources are utilized more efficiently and
responsibility be fixed to ensure timely disbursement and utilization of funds at all levels.
(Para 2.2)
Action Taken
3.2 The Ministry is in agreement with the views of the Committee. There is need to enhance
the outlay for the Health sector to reduce the out of pocket expenditure burden, particularly for
the poor and unprivileged sections of the society. The Ministry is also undertaking necessary
measures to monitor and improve the efficiency of available resources and also monitor timely
disbursement of funds at all levels through CPSMS, etc.
Further Recommendation
3.3 The Committee feels that mere agreement with its views would not suffice. The
Committee would like to be informed of the steps taken so far/contemplated to be taken
in the future to reduce the out-of-pocket payments made by households in time of health
distress. The specific role which the National Health Mission would play in reducing the
exorbitant out-of-pocket expenses, may also be indicated.
Recommendation/Observation
3.4 The Committee is not able to comprehend as to how Department with the approved outlay

XI. MILLENIUM DEVELOPMENT GOALS (MDGS)
Recommendation/Observation
3.56 The Committee feels that the success rate of achievements with regard to Millennium
Development Goals has been a mixed bag of success. While the department is more or less on
track with respect to MDG-4 and MDG-5, the success rate in respect of MDG-6 seems a distant
dream especially with regard to the viral diseases like Dengue, Chikungunya which is a constant
cause of worry year after year, not to mention new diseases like H1N1 which have now started
spreading across the country. The Department should, therefore, put in place a ‘Dedicated Sentinel
Force’ whose main protocol would be ensuring prevention of entry of diseases from outside the
borders(land, sea, air) of the country. Additionally, the Committee feels that the Department should
explore the possibility of tapping the additional resources for mopping up additional funds for its
various programmes particularly for the welfare of our poverty ridden masses. (Para 11.5)
Action Taken
3.57 W ith regard to placing ‘Dedicated Sentinel Force’ in respect of vector borne diseases i.e.
Malaria, Dengue and Chikungunya, it is submitted that Malaria is endemic in all the areas of the
country except areas located above 5000 ft. from the sea level. There is routine surveillance system
to monitor the diseases status in the country. Dengue is also endemic in major part of the country
and Chikungunya has re-emerged and is being reported since 2006. To monitor the situation in the
country 347 sentinel sites have been established in the country.
3.58 A well organized programme called National Vector Borne Disease Control Programme is
being implemented throughout the country for control of vector borne diseases including Malaria,
Dengue and Chikungunya with adequate resource provisions under NRHM. At the state level, there
is a state programme officer for vector borne diseases and at district level, the district malaria
officer now renamed as district VBD officer does exist. District level officers are supported with
technical staff to perform the activities. The programme is integrated under primary health care
system at PHC level.
3.59 The achievements with respect of Millennium Development Goal are as under:
Malaria:
● Millennium Development Goals (MDG) for Malaria  is to halt and begin to reverse the
incidence of malaria and other major diseases by 2015.
● Prevalence and death rates associated with Malaria.
● Proportion population in Malaria risk areas using effective Malaria prevention and
treatment measures (Percentage of population covered under Indoor Residual Spray
(IRS)).
● The incidence of malaria in the country started halting and sustaining reversal of cases
for last one decade. The malaria cases were brought down from 2,031,790 cases in
2000 to 1,816,569 cases in 2005 and further brought down to 1,066,972 cases in
2012. Country is heading towards achieving target of 50% reduction in incidence of
malaria cases against the baseline.

82
· The malaria death rate in the country was 0.09 deaths per lakh population in 2000
which has come down to 0.04 deaths per lakh population in 2012 as per
Annexure-VII.
· The annual incidence has been constantly declining, which reveals that the malaria
incidence has already been halted and being reversed, as indicated at table given above.
Dengue:
3.60 Dengue is an outbreak prone mosquito transmitted viral disease and is one of the neglected
tropical diseases. There is neither any drug nor any vaccine available as on date against Dengue
infection. In India, the risk of dengue has shown an increase since 2000 due to demographic and
societal changes leading to unplanned and uncontrolled urbanization and concurrent population
growth which has put severe constraints on civic amenities, particularly water supply and solid
waste disposal, thereby increasing the breeding potential of the vector species. Dengue has the
potential of causing large scale outbreaks. Though the incidence of Dengue cases has been
increased, however, the case fatality rate (CFR) i.e. death per 100 cases has been declined since

XII. IMPLEMENTATION OF NRHM (PHASE-I)
3.63 The Department has delineated the following issues during the implementation of NRHM
(Phase-I):
Problem Areas :
State Government:-
● Low capacities to manage large programmes especially in Empowered Action Group
(EAG) States. The contribution of block level and district level planning structure and
PRI in the planning process was inadequate.
● Inadequate capacities across many States to carry out infrastructure planning and
implementation e.g. lack of dedicated/exclusive civil construction wing especially under
NRHM and lack of systems with regards to external evaluation and monitoring of
construction works taken up across States.
● Non-availability and uneven distribution of skilled health care provider including critical
manpower like specialists, nurses etc. especially in EAG States is a challenge. High

84
attrition rates of HR, due to lack of clear cut HR Policies and inadequate career
progression opportunities. Deployment of health HR has not been fully rationalized as
there is inadequate deployment in underserved, remote and tribal areas.
● Convergence issues with various implementation agencies like ICDS, education
department, water and sanitation and rural development. Lack of coordination among
frontline providers (ANM, AWW, ASHA) for delivering services towards common goal
of health.
● There is no clear cut policy and systems to provide free generic medicines in public
health facilities across States. Also, States lack adequate Institutional mechanism for
procurement, and supply chain management of drugs. Many States are lacking
rationalized Essential Drugs List (EDL) and published drug formulary.
● Delay in the registration and cash disbursement to beneficiaries under JSY .
● There may be inadequate coordination between the State Health Society and the State
Health Department. Also, insufficient tenure of Mission directors causes leadership
deficit.
Private
● NRHM continues to improve outreach mainly through strengthening of public sector
health facilities and the involvement of private sector is presently limited to a few areas
such as Blindness Control, RNTCP, family planning institutional deliveries and patient
transport. However, the presence of private sector in rural areas, particularly in remote
locations, is negligible.
Action Taken
● States have involved PRIs in the implementation of health and family welfare
programme through progressive transfer of funds clear articulation of functions and by
training equipping and empowering them suitably to manage and supervise the
functioning of health facilities.
● Technical support agencies like NHSRC and SHSRC have been created at National and
State levels to provide handholding support to the States to aid Decentralized planning.
● States are now required to report the progress of construction works as part of
mandatory disclosures on their respective NRHM websites.
● As per conditionalities laid down in ROP 2012-13 States are required to carry out
rational deployment of HR with the highest priority accorded to high focus districts
and delivery points/priority facilities and on compliance would lead to reduction of up
to 7 V2% of total funds.
● There are policies in many States for monetary compensation (direct and indirect
financial incentives) to Doctors/Paramedics for serving in hand to reach and difficult
areas.
● As per conditionalities laid down in ROP 2012-13 States are incentivized for policy and
systems for providing free generic medicines to all in public health facilities (incentive
upto 5% of MFP). States have been provided support for procurement and logistics
management of drugs.

85
● To address the issue of interdepartmental coordination common review meeting are
being held between representatives from various social sector departments. Also
VHNDS and fixed immunization days are being conducted in Anganwadi centres.
● States are being supported to set up a integrated call centre which would create a
network of ambulances running under State budget, PPP and others to provide
comprehensive referral and emergency transport services.
● States are being supported to create dedicated infrastructure development teams and set
up robust procurement and logistics systems.
● Best practices are being shared across States.
● To provide more human resources for health, medical seats for undergraduate and post
graduate doctors are being increased through creating more medical colleges and
increasing seats in existing medical colleges specifically focusing in underserved areas.
Similarly, more GNM/ANM schools are proposed to be opened during Twelfth five
year plan. (Para 12.1)
Action Taken
3.64 Matter of Record.
Recommendation/Observation
3.65 From perusal of the above, the Committee finds that the major problem in implementation
of the NRHM (Phase-I) stems from lack of adequate infrastructure/manpower in the States/UTs,
which has a direct impact on the implementation of the Mission on the whole. The Committee,
while welcoming the initiatives being taken by the Department to increase involvement of the
States, feels that the Department should first and foremost focus on ensuring opening of more
medical colleges, district hospitals, GNM/ANM schools without further delay along with ensuring
that such colleges/schools are opened on equitable distribution throughout the country so as to
ensure that the Department’s Goal to ensure Universal Health Coverage is implemented in both letter
and spirit. (Para 12.2)
Action Taken
3.66 An amount of Rs. 616.51 crore has been released to states so far for opening of 200 ANM/
GNM schools. The State Governments have been asked to implement programmes for opening of
schools without delay.
Further Recommendation
3.67 The Committee strongly observes that the Department should not get complacent by
releasing funds to the States and instead follow-up and constantly monitor the utilization of
funds. State Governments may be impressed upon the need to send proposals.
XIII. NEW SCHEMES DURING TWELFTH PLAN
Recommendation/Observation
3.68 The Committee, while being appreciative of the New Schemes being launched during the
Twelfth Plan, would like the Department to focus aggressively on provision of free generic drugs
as the high Out of Pocket Expenditure still remains a major cause of concern for the vast majority

86
of people in the country. The Committee also impress that the Department should also encourage
production of more generic drugs, as manufacture of Generic Drugs by the Department and free
provision of the same by the Government would reduce the high Out of Pocket Expenses that a
vast majority of the people still bear with. (Para 13.3)
Action Taken
3.69 As per Twelfth Plan Document approved by National Development Council (NDC),
“Availability of essential medicines in public sector health facilities free of cost is critical to achieve
affordable health care for the bulk of the population. This is the area which provides the speediest
scope for improved service delivery in return for allocation of sufficient resources. A set of
measures including revision and expansion of the Essential Drugs List, ensuring the rational use of
drugs, strengthening the drug regulatory system, and supporting the setting up of national and state
drug supply logistics corporations is being recommended as core components. State would be
encouraged to plan and partially fund universal access to essential drugs and diagnostic services
in all government health care facilities. Drug supply would be linked to centralized procurement at
state level to ensure inform drug quality and cost minimization by removing intermediaries.” The
total outlay during the Twelfth Five Year plan period is Rs. 16000 crores. The basic implementation
framework of the scheme is being prepared and has not been finalized so far.
Further Recommendation
3.70 The Committee recommend that the Department should move faster for
implementation of the said Scheme as the second year of the Twelfth Plan is already in
progress and still the basic implementation framework of the scheme is being prepared and
has not been finalized so far.

PREFACE
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Health and
Family Welfare, having been authorized by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf,
present this Seventy-ninth Report of the Committee on the Drugs and Cosmetics (Amendment) Bill,
2013*.
2. In pursuance of Rule 270 of the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in the
Council of States relating to the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committees, the
Chairman, Rajya Sabha, referred** the Drugs and Cosmetics (Amendment) Bill, 2013  (Annexure-I)
as introduced in the Rajya Sabha on the 29
th August, 2013 to the Committee on the 9 th September,
2013 for examination and report by 8 th November, 2013. Subsequently, the Committee was granted
extension of time till 18 th December, 2013.
3. The Committee issued a Press Release inviting memoranda/views from individuals and other
stakeholders ( Annexure-II) . In response thereto 73 Memoranda from individuals and others
relevant to the Bill were received. List of individuals from whom memoranda were received is at
Annexure-III .
4.  The Committee held eight sittings during the course of examination of the Bill namely
26
th September, 12 th November, 21 st November, 22 nd November, 29 th November, 9 th December,
16th December and 17 th December, 2013. The list of witnesses heard by the Committee is at
Annexure-IV .
5. The Committee considered the draft Report on 16 th and 17 th December, 2013 and adopted
the same on 17 th December, 2013.
6. The Committee has relied on the following documents in finalizing the Report.
(i) The Drugs and Cosmetics (Amendment) Bill, 2013;
(ii) Background Notes on the Bill received from the Department of Health and Family
Welfare;
(iii) Presentation, clarifications and Oral evidence of Secretary, Department of Health and
Family Welfare;
(iv) Memoranda received on the Bill from various institutes/bodies/associations/
organizations/experts and replies of the Ministry on the memoranda selected by the
Committee for examination.
(v) Oral evidence and written submissions by various stakeholders/experts from various
medical professions, on the Bill; and
(vi) Replies to the questions/queries raised by Members in the meeting on the Bill received
from the Department of Health and Family Welfare.
* Published in Gazette of India Extraordinary Part II Section 2, dated 29 th August, 2013.
** Rajya Sabha Parliamentary Bulletin Part II, No.51252, dated 9 th September, 2013.

7. On behalf of the Committee, I would like to acknowledge with thanks the contributions
made by those who deposed before the Committee and also those who gave their valuable
suggestions to the Committee through their written submissions.
8. For facility of reference and convenience, the observations and recommendations of the
Committee have been printed in bold letters in the body of the Report.
